title: Causal Learning Handbook
text:
Welcome!
This handbook introduces the Causal Roadmap, Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), and Super Learner for modern causal inference in epidemiology, with an emphasis on pharmacoepidemiology and clinical trial analysis. Each chapter builds on the previous ones, with worked R code examples throughout.
This handbook was developed by Andrew Mertens as part of work for the UC Berkeley Center for Targeted Machine Learning and Causal Inference. For questions, suggestions, or bug reports, please contact Andrew at amertens@berkeley.edu.

title: Causal Learning Handbook
text:
0.1 Who is this book for?
This handbook is written for analysts who already know how to fit regression models in R and now need to do causal analysis on observational health data, primarily pharmacoepidemiologists, biostatisticians, and epidemiologists working on drug effectiveness, safety, and real-world evidence. The worked examples assume comfort with R and basic regression; they do not assume prior exposure to potential-outcomes notation, targeted learning, or g-methods.
The book is not a substitute for a foundational causal inference text (for that, and other useful references, see the Other Resources page), but it is intended to be self-contained for someone working through a longitudinal real-world-data analysis from scratch. A Glossary is provided in the appendix for the abbreviations and short technical terms used throughout.

title: Causal Learning Handbook
text:
0.2 How to use this book
Short on time? Start with the Short Course. It covers the Causal Roadmap, TMLE (by hand and with software), and longitudinal causal inference in a single chapter. You can work through it in about an hour and come away with a working understanding of the core framework.
Want the full treatment? Read the handbook front-to-back. The chapters are organized into six parts. Part I builds the conceptual foundations: why standard regression is not enough for causal questions, and how the Causal Roadmap structures an analysis. Part II walks through each major estimation strategy with hands-on code. Part III extends to longitudinal settings with time-varying confounding, longitudinal TMLE (L-TMLE), and Longitudinal Modified Treatment Policies (LMTP). Part IV covers diagnostics and sensitivity analysis. Part V is an end-to-end applied workflow built around the lmtp package. Part VI addresses special topics including effect heterogeneity, mediation, hybrid RCT/RWD designs, and time-to-event estimands. A short Synthesis part then revisits the running case study, and the appendices collect a glossary, an annotated bibliography, and external resources.
You can also jump to specific chapters as needed. Each chapter is self-contained enough to be read independently, though they build on each other.

Description




Regression vs. Causal Inference
Why a regression coefficient for a treatment is not, on its own, a causal effect; the counterfactual (“what if everyone had been treated?”) framework; and the “Table 2 fallacy”, interpreting every adjusted coefficient in a regression output as a causal effect for its own variable.

Chapter
Description




G-Computation
Outcome modeling and standardization: fit a model for the outcome, predict each person’s outcome under each treatment value, and average across the sample.


IPTW
Inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting: weight each individual by the inverse of their probability of receiving the treatment they actually got, so the weighted sample mimics one in which treatment was randomized. Covers stabilized weights, truncation, and diagnostics.


Doubly Robust Estimation and TMLE
Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) and Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE): combining outcome and treatment models for double robustness.


Super Learner
Ensemble machine learning for nuisance estimation and integration with TMLE.

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
3 The Causal Roadmap
From roadmap to TMLE to longitudinal methods in one chapter
Estimated reading time: 60 minutes
This chapter is a self-contained short course that walks through the core ideas of the handbook in a single sitting. It covers the Causal Roadmap, point-treatment TMLE (by hand and with software), longitudinal causal inference, and the lmtp package for realistic interventions. Each section is concise; the full handbook chapters provide deeper treatment.
It is tempting to load the data and start fitting models. The roadmap resists that, because the model you reach for silently decides which question you end up answering. Working through a fixed sequence keeps the scientific question, rather than the software, in charge. Every causal analysis in this handbook follows the same seven steps:
The key insight: the causal question and estimand are defined before any model is fit. The estimand determines which statistical quantity to target. The estimation method is chosen to match that target.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
3.1 Identification: three assumptions
Under three assumptions, the causal estimand equals a function of the observed data:

Consistency: the observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment actually received. Treatment must be well-defined.
Exchangeability: conditional on measured covariates \(W\), treatment is independent of potential outcomes. No unmeasured confounders.
Positivity: every covariate stratum has a nonzero probability of receiving each treatment. \(0 < P(A = a \mid W) < 1\).

Under these assumptions, the average treatment effect is identified by:
\[
E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = E_W\!\left[E[Y \mid A=1, W] - E[Y \mid A=0, W]\right]
\]
This is the g-computation formula. It says: model the outcome within levels of treatment and covariates, then average over the covariate distribution.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
4.1 Setup: simulated clinical trial data


Show code
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000

# Baseline covariates
age <- rnorm(n, 65, 10)
cvd <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.03 * age))

# Treatment (confounded by age and CVD history)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.02 * age + 0.5 * cvd))

# Outcome (binary: adverse event)
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2.5 + 0.03 * age + 0.5 * cvd - 0.4 * A))

dat <- tibble(age, cvd, A, Y)
cat("n =", n, ", treatment rate:", round(mean(A), 2),
    ", outcome rate:", round(mean(Y), 2), "\n")
#> n = 1000 , treatment rate: 0.75 , outcome rate: 0.35
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
4.2 G-computation in three steps
G-computation is the simplest causal estimator. It implements the identification formula directly.


Show code
# Step 1: Fit outcome model
Qmod <- glm(Y ~ A + age + cvd, family = binomial, data = dat)

# Step 2: Predict under each treatment for everyone
Q1 <- predict(Qmod, newdata = mutate(dat, A = 1), type = "response")
Q0 <- predict(Qmod, newdata = mutate(dat, A = 0), type = "response")

# Step 3: Average (standardize)
gcomp_ate <- mean(Q1) - mean(Q0)
cat("G-computation ATE:", round(gcomp_ate, 4), "\n")
#> G-computation ATE: -0.0454


G-computation depends entirely on the outcome model. If that model is wrong, the estimate is biased and nothing downstream repairs it. Two ideas in the rest of this section address that: a flexible way to fit the models (Super Learner), and an estimator that stays consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is right (TMLE).
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
4.3 TMLE by hand
TMLE adds a targeting step that corrects the outcome model using the propensity score. This makes it doubly robust: consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified. The correction nudges the initial predictions hardest for patients whose treatment was least expected given their covariates, which is where the outcome model is most likely to be wrong; the propensity score enters only through that nudge, the clever covariate H below.


Show code
logit <- function(p) log(p / (1 - p))

# Step 1: Initial outcome predictions (already done above)
Qinit <- predict(Qmod, type = "response")

# Step 2: Estimate propensity score
gmod <- glm(A ~ age + cvd, family = binomial, data = dat)
ps <- predict(gmod, type = "response")
ps <- pmax(0.01, pmin(0.99, ps))  # bound away from 0/1

# Step 3: Clever covariate
H <- dat$A / ps - (1 - dat$A) / (1 - ps)

# Step 4: Fluctuation (the targeting step)
epsilon <- glm(dat$Y ~ -1 + offset(logit(Qinit)) + H,
               family = binomial)$coef

# Update counterfactual predictions
H1 <- 1 / ps
H0 <- -1 / (1 - ps)
Q1_star <- plogis(logit(Q1) + epsilon * H1)
Q0_star <- plogis(logit(Q0) + epsilon * H0)

# TMLE estimate
tmle_ate <- mean(Q1_star) - mean(Q0_star)
cat("TMLE ATE:", round(tmle_ate, 4), "\n")
#> TMLE ATE: -0.0578


The fluctuation parameter \(\hat{\epsilon}\) captures how much the treatment model corrects the outcome model. If the outcome model is already well-calibrated for the ATE, \(\hat{\epsilon}\) is near zero.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
section: 4.4 Inference from the efficient influence curve
text:
4.4 Inference from the efficient influence curve
Each patient contributes one number to the estimate, the patient’s value of the efficient influence curve. The estimate behaves like the average of those numbers, so its standard error is their standard deviation divided by the square root of n, and a few patients with extreme values are what widen the interval.


Show code
# Efficient influence curve
Qstar_obs <- ifelse(dat$A == 1, Q1_star, Q0_star)
H_obs <- ifelse(dat$A == 1, H1, H0)
EIC <- H_obs * (dat$Y - Qstar_obs) + Q1_star - Q0_star - tmle_ate

# Standard error and 95% CI
se <- sqrt(var(EIC) / n)
ci <- tmle_ate + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

cat("ATE:", round(tmle_ate, 4), "\n")
#> ATE: -0.0578
cat("SE: ", round(se, 4), "\n")
#> SE:  0.0366
cat("95% CI: [", round(ci[1], 4), ",", round(ci[2], 4), "]\n")
#> 95% CI: [ -0.1297 , 0.014 ]
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
section: 4.5 Super Learner: flexible models for the nuisances
text:
4.5 Super Learner: flexible models for the nuisances
The code above fit the outcome and treatment models with glm, which assumes the relationships are linear on the logit scale. When they are not, both nuisance estimates are biased, and so is the causal estimate. Super Learner replaces a single guessed model with a library of candidate algorithms, for example a logistic regression, a spline model, and a random forest, and uses cross-validation to weight them by how well each predicts data it did not see. The ensemble is, in large samples, about as accurate as the best candidate in the library, without the analyst having to know in advance which that is. In a targeted-learning analysis Super Learner estimates the nuisance models and TMLE does the targeting on top; the software call below sets this up through its Q.SL.library and g.SL.library arguments.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
4.6 Software implementation
The tmle package automates all of this, including Super Learner for flexible nuisance estimation:


Show code
library(tmle)

result <- tmle(
  Y = dat$Y, A = dat$A,
  W = dat[, c("age", "cvd")],
  Q.SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"),
  g.SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean")
)
result
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
5.1 The problem: treatment-confounder feedback
In longitudinal settings, a time-varying confounder (like CD4 count) can be both a confounder of future treatment and a consequence of past treatment. Standard regression cannot handle both roles simultaneously: adjusting for CD4 blocks the treatment’s indirect effect through CD4, while not adjusting leaves confounding.
This is treatment-confounder feedback, and it requires g-methods.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
5.2 Simulated longitudinal data


Show code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 2000

# Baseline
W_age <- rnorm(n, 40, 10)
W_male <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.6)
W_cd4_bl <- pmax(50, rnorm(n, 350, 120))
W_vl_bl <- rnorm(n, 4.2, 0.7)
W <- 0.01 * (W_age - 40) - 0.001 * (W_cd4_bl - 350) + 0.2 * W_vl_bl - 0.1 * W_male

# Visit 1
A1 <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.3 + 0.5 * W))
L1 <- rnorm(n, mean = 0.3 * W + 1.2 * A1, sd = 1)  # treatment affects confounder

# Visit 2 (confounder affects future treatment)
A2 <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.8 * L1 + 0.3 * A1))

# Outcome
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.8 - 0.4 * A1 - 0.5 * A2 - 0.6 * L1 + 0.2 * W))
dat_long <- tibble(W, A1, L1, A2, Y)
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
5.3 Longitudinal G-computation by hand
The backwards sequential regression resolves the feedback. At time 2, condition on \(L_1\) to deconfound \(A_2\). At time 1, do NOT condition on \(L_1\) to preserve the mediated effect.


Show code
# Oracle truth
set.seed(9999)
n_mc <- 100000; W_mc <- rep(W, length.out = n_mc)
L1_cf <- rnorm(n_mc, mean = 0.3 * W_mc + 1.2, sd = 1)
true_EY_11 <- mean(plogis(-0.8 - 0.4 - 0.5 - 0.6 * L1_cf + 0.2 * W_mc))

# Step 1: Model outcome at time 2, conditioning on L1
Q2_mod <- glm(Y ~ A2 + L1 + A1 + W, family = binomial, data = dat_long)
Q2_A2is1 <- predict(Q2_mod, newdata = mutate(dat_long, A2 = 1), type = "response")

# Step 2: Backwards regression: model Q2 predictions WITHOUT L1
Q1_mod <- glm(Q2_A2is1 ~ A1 + W, family = quasibinomial, data = dat_long)
Q1_A1is1 <- predict(Q1_mod, newdata = mutate(dat_long, A1 = 1), type = "response")

gcomp_long <- mean(Q1_A1is1)

# Compare to naive regression (which conditions on L1 throughout)
naive_mod <- glm(Y ~ A1 + A2 + L1 + W, family = binomial, data = dat_long)
naive_pred <- mean(predict(naive_mod,
  newdata = mutate(dat_long, A1 = 1, A2 = 1), type = "response"))

cat("True E[Y(1,1)]:     ", round(true_EY_11, 4), "\n")
#> True E[Y(1,1)]:      0.0941
cat("Naive (biased):      ", round(naive_pred, 4), "\n")
#> Naive (biased):       0.1411
cat("G-computation (long):", round(gcomp_long, 4), "\n")
#> G-computation (long): 0.1125


The naive estimate is biased because it conditions on \(L_1\) (blocking part of the treatment effect). The backwards G-computation avoids this.
Longitudinal TMLE adds a targeting step to each of these backwards regressions, the same fluctuation idea as in the point-treatment case, applied at every time point. This buys sequential double robustness: the estimate is consistent if, at each step, either the outcome regression or the treatment model is correct. The mechanics are developed in Chapter 14; here we turn to the kind of intervention that longitudinal data make possible.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning
text:
5.4 LMTP for realistic interventions
Static regimes (“always treat”) often violate positivity. The lmtp package estimates modified treatment policies that shift treatment by a feasible amount.


Show code
library(lmtp)

# Shift function: increase adherence by 10 percentage points
shift_up <- function(data, trt) pmin(data[[trt]] + 0.10, 1.0)

# Natural course (no intervention)
shift_none <- function(data, trt) data[[trt]]

# Estimate under each regime
fit_shifted <- lmtp_tmle(
  data = my_data,
  trt = paste0("PDC_", 1:4),
  outcome = paste0("Y_", 1:4),
  baseline = c("W0", "A0"),
  time_vary = lapply(1:4, function(t) paste0("L_", t)),
  shift = shift_up,
  mtp = TRUE,
  outcome_type = "survival",
  learners_outcome = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"),
  learners_trt = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"),
  folds = 2
)

# Contrast vs natural course
contrast <- lmtp_contrast(fit_shifted, ref = fit_natural, type = "additive")
contrast


The shift function defines the intervention: increase each patient’s adherence by 10 percentage points at each visit, capped at 1.0. This stays within the observed data support because no patient is assigned an impossible adherence level. The mtp = TRUE flag tells lmtp that the shifted value depends on the natural treatment value.
crumbs: 2  Short Course: Causal Inference with Targeted Learning

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.1 Clinical and epidemiologic motivation
Estimated reading time: 20 minutes
Throughout this handbook, we use a single recurring causal question to illustrate causal concepts, estimation methods, and diagnostic tools: does initiating highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) reduce mortality among people living with HIV, and if so, by how much? We answer this question using a simulated longitudinal HIV antiretroviral therapy cohort built to reflect the marginal structural model literature, distributed in the ipw R package (Wal and Geskus 2011). Anchoring every chapter to the same question and dataset lets you see how each method approaches the same target, and makes it easier to compare results across approaches.
In the early years of combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART), a central clinical question was: does initiating HAART reduce mortality among HIV-positive patients, and if so, by how much? Although this sounds like a question about HAART “use,” it is really a question about strategies for when to start HAART, because therapy is initiated (and then sustained) in response to evolving clinical status. The longitudinal, time-dependent nature of the initiation decision is what creates the confounding structure we have to address.
Answering this from observational data is harder than it looks. Physicians do not assign HAART randomly. They initiate therapy when CD4 cell counts decline and clinical status worsens. The very biomarkers that predict death also determine who gets treated and when. This is confounding by indication. The sickest patients get the strongest drugs, so a naive comparison can make the best medicines look like poison.
The problem runs deeper than baseline confounding. HAART, once initiated, improves CD4 counts. A patient’s CD4 level at any given visit therefore reflects both their underlying disease trajectory and the effects of prior treatment. CD4 count is simultaneously a confounder of future treatment decisions and a mediator of past treatment effects. This treatment-confounder feedback is the defining feature of the dataset and the reason it motivates the longitudinal g-methods developed in later chapters.
The dataset we use is a simulated cohort of 1,200 HIV-positive patients designed to reflect the structure of real HIV cohort studies. Because the data-generating process is known, we can compare estimation methods and understand exactly where simpler approaches fail.
crumbs: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.2 Why this example is useful
Four features make this cohort a good teaching vehicle. The confounding by indication described above is severe enough that HAART initiators look worse than non-initiators in a crude analysis, simply because they had lower CD4 and worse prognosis when they started, so the cohort shows plainly how an effective treatment can appear harmful. The treatment-confounder feedback through CD4 means no single regression can both adjust for CD4 and preserve its role as a mediator, which is what forces the longitudinal g-methods. The analysis also demands a clearly specified target trial and estimand before any model is fit, because vague causal questions produce numerically precise answers that cannot be interpreted against any well-defined contrast. Finally, the functional forms are unknown: how age, sex, and the evolving CD4 jointly drive both the treatment decision and mortality is plausibly non-linear and interactive, for instance if risk rises sharply only once CD4 falls below a threshold, or if a low CD4 weighs differently on the initiation decision at different ages. Committing to one parametric form risks the misspecification bias shown in Chapter 6, which is why the nuisance models are estimated with Super Learner (Chapter 9) rather than a single guessed regression.
crumbs: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.3 The observed data
The dataset is distributed as haartdat in the ipw R package (Wal and Geskus 2011). It is a simulated cohort (not a prospective study) built to reproduce the structure of real HIV cohorts used in the marginal structural model literature. It contains 1,200 HIV-positive patients observed from HIV seroconversion in person-period (long) format, with one row per patient per fixed 100-day interval. The regular interval grid is a feature of the simulation; in real-world data, visit times would be irregular and would themselves need to be modeled.


Show code
library(ipw)
library(tidyverse)
data(haartdat)



3.3.1 Variable dictionary








Variable
Description
Role




patient
Patient identifier (1 to 1,200)
Unit of analysis


tstart
Start of time interval (days since seroconversion)
Time structure


fuptime
End of time interval (days since seroconversion)
Time structure


haartind
HAART indicator: 1 if HAART has been initiated by the end of this interval, 0 otherwise
Time-varying treatment (A)


event
Death indicator: 1 if patient died during this interval
Outcome (Y)


sex
Sex: 0 = male, 1 = female
Baseline confounder (W)


age
Age in years at follow-up start
Baseline confounder (W)


cd4.sqrt
Square root of CD4 cell count at the end of the interval
Time-varying confounder (L)


endtime
Patient’s final observed time (days)
Administrative variable


dropout
Censoring indicator: 1 if patient dropped out at interval end
Censoring (C)



Each patient contributes between 1 and 38 rows (median approximately 15), corresponding to 100-day intervals from seroconversion through up to day 3,700. The treatment variable haartind is absorbing: once a patient initiates HAART, it stays 1 for all subsequent intervals. Among the 1,200 patients, 376 (31%) initiate HAART during follow-up. The key time-varying confounder is cd4.sqrt, measured at the start of each interval before the treatment and censoring decisions that occur at the interval’s end. This temporal ordering, CD4 measured first, then treatment and outcome, is what makes causal identification possible under the sequential exchangeability assumption.


3.3.2 Example patient trajectories


Show code
example_ids <- c(1, 5, 10)

# Find first HAART initiation time for each patient
haart_start <- haartdat |>
  filter(patient %in% example_ids, haartind == 1) |>
  group_by(patient) |>
  summarise(haart_time = min(fuptime), .groups = "drop")

haartdat |>
  filter(patient %in% example_ids) |>
  mutate(cd4 = cd4.sqrt^2) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fuptime, y = cd4)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(haartind)), size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(
    data = haart_start |> mutate(cd4 = NA),
    aes(xintercept = haart_time),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("Patient", patient), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("0" = "grey50", "1" = "steelblue"),
    labels = c("Pre-HAART", "On HAART"),
    name = "Treatment status"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Follow-up time (days since seroconversion)",
    y = "CD4 count (cells/\u00B5L)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 3.1: CD4 trajectories for three example patients. Vertical dashed lines mark the interval at which each patient initiates HAART (haartind switches from 0 to 1). Patient 1 initiates relatively early and has a rising CD4 trajectory afterward. Patients who initiate later show different pre-treatment CD4 patterns, illustrating the confounding-by-indication structure: treatment timing depends on the evolving CD4 trajectory.





The figure shows CD4 trajectories on the original (back-transformed) scale. Each patient initiates HAART at a different time, and CD4 counts fluctuate throughout follow-up. This is the longitudinal, time-varying structure that makes causal inference challenging: treatment timing depends on the evolving CD4 trajectory, and treatment itself changes the trajectory.


3.3.3 Cohort summary of baseline characteristics
Several chapters (g-computation, IPTW, point-treatment TMLE) work with a simpler point-treatment version of the question, contrasting ever versus never initiating HAART using only baseline confounders. For those chapters we collapse the longitudinal data into a baseline snapshot with one row per patient:


Show code
haart_baseline <- haartdat |>
  group_by(patient) |>
  summarise(
    sex = first(sex),
    age = first(age),
    cd4_baseline = first(cd4.sqrt)^2,
    cd4_sqrt_baseline = first(cd4.sqrt),
    ever_haart = max(haartind),
    died = max(event),
    dropout = max(dropout),
    total_fup_days = max(fuptime),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

haart_baseline |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pct_female = mean(sex) * 100,
    median_age = median(age),
    median_cd4 = median(cd4_baseline),
    pct_ever_haart = mean(ever_haart) * 100,
    pct_died = mean(died) * 100,
    pct_dropout = mean(dropout) * 100
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Baseline cohort summary")

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.4 The causal question
The primary causal question is:

Among HIV-positive individuals under longitudinal follow-up from seroconversion, what would the risk of death have been under a strategy of initiating HAART when clinically indicated, compared with a strategy of never initiating HAART during follow-up?

“Clinically indicated” here means a CD4-driven initiation rule consistent with the guidance in force during the cohort era; for concreteness, initiate HAART at the first interval at which CD4 falls below a fixed threshold (e.g., 350 cells/µL) and continue thereafter.
It is worth being explicit about what this threshold is and is not. The threshold defines the intervention regime we want to evaluate, the counterfactual strategy whose mortality risk we are estimating. It does not describe the policy under which the observed data were generated: in the haartdat simulation, HAART initiation is not triggered by a hard CD4 cutoff but by a probabilistic model in which the hazard of initiating increases as CD4 falls (and also depends on age and sex). The whole point of the causal analysis is to estimate what would have happened under the cleaner threshold-based strategy, despite the fact that the observed initiation process is a noisier, covariate-driven one.
The comparator strategy, “never initiate HAART,” is the static contrast used in the marginal structural model literature and the longitudinal analogue of the ever vs never contrast used in Chapter 6–Chapter 8 (where the point-treatment chapters collapse the longitudinal data to a baseline snapshot and ask “ever initiated vs never initiated”). The dynamic-vs-static framing here is deliberate: a single regression cannot estimate the dynamic arm without inducing bias, which is the failure mode that motivates the g-methods developed in Part III. Readers interested in the clinically most relevant contrast (comparing two CD4-driven initiation strategies against each other, e.g., initiate at CD4 < 350 vs initiate at CD4 < 200) will find that dynamic-vs-dynamic comparison developed in Chapter 14 and Chapter 14.
This is a question about sustained treatment strategies, not a single-timepoint comparison of treated versus untreated patients. The causal question asks what would happen if we could assign treatment strategies to everyone, removing the influence of confounding on the treatment decision. The associational question, by contrast, compares patients who happened to initiate HAART with those who did not, and that comparison is confounded because sicker patients are more likely to start treatment.
crumbs: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.5 The target trial
To make the causal question precise, we specify the randomized trial we would ideally conduct. This target trial protocol serves as a design template that the observational analysis attempts to emulate.







Component
Specification




Eligibility
HIV-positive adults at seroconversion, antiretroviral-naive


Time zero
Date of HIV seroconversion


Treatment strategies
(1) Initiate HAART at the first interval at which CD4 falls below the contemporaneous clinical threshold (e.g., 350 cells/µL) and continue thereafter, vs. (2) never initiate HAART during follow-up


Assignment
Random assignment to strategy at time zero


Outcome
All-cause mortality


Follow-up
From seroconversion until death, dropout, or administrative end of study (up to 3,700 days)


Causal contrast
Risk difference in mortality at a specified time horizon


Analysis
Per-protocol: we estimate the effect of adhering to each sustained strategy, since the scientific question is about treatment strategies rather than randomized assignment. An ITT analogue is not natural in an observational target-trial emulation because there is no baseline randomization to be “intended.” Chapter 5 discusses the ITT-vs-per-protocol choice as part of the Causal Roadmap, and Chapter 14 walks through how the per-protocol effect is identified from observational data via g-methods.



The target trial forces us to define the causal question before choosing a statistical method. It makes the assumptions transparent: we are asking what would have happened under specific, well-defined treatment strategies. And it highlights where the observational data fall short of the ideal, since treatment is not randomly assigned but determined by evolving clinical status. The causal roadmap (Chapter 5) provides the framework for bridging from this ideal trial to the data we actually have.

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.6 Causal structure

3.6.1 A simplified DAG for point-treatment chapters
For the early chapters (g-computation, IPTW, TMLE), we work with a point-treatment simplification where treatment is “ever initiated HAART” and confounders are measured at baseline:


Show code
library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)

simple_dag <- dagify(
  A ~ W_age + W_sex + W_cd4,
  Y ~ A + W_age + W_sex + W_cd4,
  exposure = "A",
  outcome = "Y",
  coords = list(
    x = c(W_age = 0, W_sex = 0, W_cd4 = 0, A = 1, Y = 2),
    y = c(W_age = 1.5, W_sex = 1, W_cd4 = 0.5, A = 0, Y = 0)
  ),
  labels = c(
    W_age = "Age", W_sex = "Sex", W_cd4 = "Baseline\nCD4",
    A = "HAART\ninitiation", Y = "Death"
  )
)

ggdag(simple_dag, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title = "Point-treatment DAG")








Figure 3.2: Simplified point-treatment DAG for the HAART example. Baseline confounders (age, sex, CD4) affect both treatment and mortality.





Under the assumptions of consistency, exchangeability (conditional on baseline confounders), and positivity, the causal effect of HAART initiation on mortality is identified by the g-computation formula.


3.6.2 The longitudinal DAG: treatment-confounder feedback
The real complexity becomes apparent in the longitudinal structure. The following DAG shows two time slices and illustrates the treatment-confounder feedback loop:


Show code
long_dag <- dagify(
  L1 ~ W,
  A1 ~ L1 + W,
  L2 ~ A1 + L1 + W,
  A2 ~ L2 + A1 + W,
  Y ~ A2 + A1 + L2 + L1 + W,
  C ~ L2 + A1 + W,
  exposure = "A1",
  outcome = "Y",
  coords = list(
    x = c(W = 0, L1 = 1, A1 = 2, L2 = 3, A2 = 4, Y = 5.5, C = 4.5),
    y = c(W = 1, L1 = 1, A1 = 0, L2 = 1, A2 = 0, Y = 0, C = 1.5)
  ),
  labels = c(
    W = "Baseline\n(age, sex)",
    L1 = "CD4(t)",
    A1 = "HAART(t)",
    L2 = "CD4(t+1)",
    A2 = "HAART(t+1)",
    Y = "Death",
    C = "Dropout"
  )
)

ggdag(long_dag, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title = "Longitudinal DAG with treatment-confounder feedback")








Figure 3.3: Longitudinal DAG for the HAART example showing treatment-confounder feedback. CD4 at time t is affected by prior HAART and also affects future HAART decisions.





The arrow from HAART(t) to CD4(t+1) represents the effect of treatment on the confounder. The arrow from CD4(t+1) to HAART(t+1) represents the confounder influencing future treatment. This is treatment-confounder feedback: CD4 is simultaneously a confounder of future treatment and a consequence of past treatment. Dropout may depend on CD4 levels and prior treatment, creating the potential for informative censoring.
This feedback structure is why later chapters need longitudinal g-methods. No single regression model can simultaneously adjust for CD4 as a confounder and preserve its role as a mediator of treatment effects.


3.6.3 Mapping the DAG to the observed data
The person-period structure of haartdat maps directly onto this longitudinal DAG. Each row corresponds to one time slice. Within each interval, the temporal ordering is: CD4 is measured (beginning of interval), then the treatment decision and outcome/censoring occur (end of interval). The variables map as follows: cd4.sqrt is \(L_t\), haartind is \(A_t\), event is \(Y\), dropout is \(C\), and age and sex are the baseline covariates \(W\).

title: 3  Running Case Study: Antiretroviral Therapy, HIV Progression, and Longitudinal Confounding
text:
3.7 Why standard approaches can mislead
The treatment-confounder feedback structure in this cohort means that naive regression approaches, whether they ignore time-varying CD4 or adjust for it, can produce misleading estimates of the HAART effect. A crude comparison of treated and untreated patients is confounded by indication (sicker patients start HAART). Adjusting for baseline covariates alone ignores that CD4 changes over time. And adjusting for time-varying CD4 in a pooled regression blocks part of the treatment’s beneficial pathway. Chapter 4 explains these failure modes in detail and motivates the g-methods (g-computation, IPTW, TMLE) that the rest of the handbook develops.

section: 3.8 Other questions this cohort will answer
text:
3.8 Other questions this cohort will answer
The mortality estimand above is the spine of the book, but the same cohort runs through the special-topics chapters, each posing a different question of the same data:

Realistic interventions, not all-or-nothing treatment. Rather than “treat everyone” versus “no one,” we can shift the adherence distribution and ask how much regimen forgiveness matters (Chapter 16), and run the full modified-treatment-policy and dynamic-rule workflow from question to estimate (Chapter 20).
The best rule, and for whom. At what CD4 threshold, and for which patients, is initiation optimal (Chapter 23)?
Effect modification. Does the benefit of HAART differ by baseline CD4 or age (Chapter 21)?
Mechanism. How much of the effect runs through CD4 recovery rather than other pathways (Chapter 24)?
Time-to-event and competing risks. Treating mortality as a survival endpoint, with non-HIV death as a competing event (Chapter 25).
Transportability. Whether an effect estimated in this cohort would carry to a different patient population (Chapter 29).

Anchoring every method to one cohort lets you see what changes when the question changes, rather than when the dataset changes.

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.1 Why Not Just Use Regression?
Estimated reading time: 25 minutes
Most observational studies start with a causal question: does treatment A reduce the risk of outcome Y compared to treatment B? Researchers typically reach for a familiar tool: fit a Cox proportional hazards model, adjust for available confounders, and interpret the hazard ratio as the answer. This workflow is so common that it can feel like the only workflow.
But there are two distinct problems with this approach. First, the regression model may be misspecified (the wrong functional form, missing interactions, or omitted confounders can bias the coefficient). Second, and more fundamentally, even a perfectly specified model may answer the wrong question. A conditional hazard ratio from a Cox model is not the same quantity as “the causal effect of treatment on 3-year risk.” The hazard ratio is a conditional, instantaneous rate measure that does not directly translate to a population-level risk difference or survival probability contrast. The causal question you want to answer may simply not correspond to any single regression coefficient.
Recognizing this gap is not a criticism of regression itself; regression remains a useful building block. The gap is a reason to adopt a more deliberate analytic workflow, a Causal Roadmap, that starts with a clearly defined causal question, specifies a target estimand on a meaningful scale (such as the risk difference or restricted mean survival time difference), and chooses an estimation strategy that targets it directly. Later chapters introduce longitudinal TMLE (L-TMLE), which can estimate causal survival curve contrasts without relying on the proportional hazards assumption.
This chapter uses a concrete clinical example to illustrate where the standard regression-only approach falls short, introduces the counterfactual framework that makes causal questions precise, and demonstrates g-computation as a first step toward targeted estimation. Later chapters build on these ideas with inverse probability weighting (IPTW), targeted minimum loss-based estimation (TMLE), and the full Causal Roadmap. The chapter proceeds as follows:
Causal conclusions require identification assumptions (consistency, exchangeability, positivity) that no statistical method can verify from data alone.
Multivariable regression has long been the standard tool in observational research for “adjusting” for confounders. But regression coefficients don’t always represent causal effects. In fact, they almost never do without additional assumptions and deliberate analytic choices that go beyond what standard regression provides.
Key point. If you’ve been trained to interpret an adjusted regression coefficient as “the effect of X on Y, holding all else equal,” you’re in good company, but that interpretation quietly smuggles in causal language that the model itself cannot justify. The coefficient tells you about the conditional association within strata defined by the other variables in the model. Whether that association equals a causal effect depends on assumptions that regression alone cannot verify.
The table-2 fallacy (Westreich and Greenland 2013) occurs when analysts interpret multiple coefficients from a single regression as if each one estimates a separate causal effect. Each coefficient in a multivariable regression has a different set of confounders, mediators, and colliders. A model that is correctly specified for the causal effect of treatment on the outcome may simultaneously produce a biased coefficient for a covariate in the same model. Treating all coefficients as causal is a common and consequential error in applied work.

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.1.1 Motivating Example: HAART and HIV Mortality
Suppose we have an observational HIV cohort and want to know whether patients who ever initiated highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) had a different risk of death than patients who never initiated it. The causal question is straightforward: if we could assign everyone in this population to HAART versus to no HAART, would the mortality risk differ, and by how much?
The standard approach is to fit a Cox proportional hazards model, adjust for confounders like age, sex, and baseline CD4 count, and report the adjusted hazard ratio. Let’s see what that looks like on the running HAART cohort (introduced in the Running Case Study and used as a point-treatment baseline snapshot here).
We adjust for age, sex, and baseline (square-root) CD4 count using a Cox model:


Show code
cox_model <- coxph(
  Surv(total_fup_days, died) ~ ever_haart + age + sex + cd4_sqrt_baseline,
  data = dat
)
tidy(cox_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Adjusted Cox proportional hazards model (hazard ratios)")

The Hazard Ratio Is NOT the Causal Effect You Want



The adjusted hazard ratio for ever_haart quantifies an instantaneous rate ratio for death within strata of age, sex, and baseline CD4. But what does a clinician or policymaker actually need to know? They need to know: if we initiated HAART in everyone eligible compared with no one, how would the cumulative mortality risk over follow-up change? That quantity, the marginal risk difference in mortality, is the natural scale for comparing treatments and making decisions.
The Cox hazard ratio does not answer that question. It is a conditional, instantaneous rate ratio that:

Assumes proportional hazards (that the treatment effect is constant over time), which is often violated in practice.
Is non-collapsible: the conditional HR and marginal HR differ even without confounding, so the coefficient does not have a straightforward population-level interpretation.
Does not directly translate to a risk difference or survival probability contrast without additional computation.
Is also confounded by indication in observational HIV data: sicker patients (lower CD4) were more likely to start HAART, so the unadjusted association conflates the drug’s benefit with baseline severity. We will return to this in the longitudinal section below.

In later chapters, we introduce longitudinal TMLE (L-TMLE), which directly estimates causal survival curves and risk differences at specific time points without relying on the proportional hazards assumption.
crumbs: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.2 Enter the Counterfactual Framework
For each person we imagine two hypothetical worlds: Y(1) (outcome if they had initiated HAART) and Y(0) (outcome if they had not) (Hernán and Robins 2025). The average treatment effect (ATE) is:
\[
ATE = E[Y(1) - Y(0)]
\]
The fundamental problem of causal inference is that each person only receives one treatment. We observe Y(1) or Y(0), never both. Under three key identification assumptions, exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding), consistency (the observed outcome under the treatment actually received equals the potential outcome), and positivity (every individual has a nonzero probability of receiving either treatment given their covariates), we can identify the causal ATE from observed data using the g-computation formula:
\[
ATE = E_W\big[ E[Y \mid A = 1, W] - E[Y \mid A = 0, W] \big]
\]
where W represents the measured confounders and A is the treatment. This expression says: within each confounder stratum, compute the difference in expected outcomes between treated and untreated, then average over the distribution of confounders in the population.
crumbs: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.3 When Regression Fails






Model Misspecification Can Silently Bias Your Results



Misspecification bias is silent. A regression with the wrong functional form still produces coefficients and p-values with no warning. This motivates semiparametric estimators (like TMLE with machine learning) that relax parametric assumptions.


Let’s compare the Cox approach to g-computation, which directly targets the marginal risk difference for mortality over follow-up. Both models are fit on the same data and adjust for the same confounders; the only thing that changes is what we ask the fitted model to report.


Show code
# G-computation: fit a logistic outcome model, then standardize
gcomp_model <- glm(
  died ~ ever_haart + age + sex + cd4_sqrt_baseline,
  family = binomial, data = dat
)

# Predict each person's counterfactual mortality risk under both strategies,
# then average to get the marginal (population-level) risks
risk1 <- mean(predict(gcomp_model, mutate(dat, ever_haart = 1), type = "response"))
risk0 <- mean(predict(gcomp_model, mutate(dat, ever_haart = 0), type = "response"))
risk_diff <- risk1 - risk0
risk_ratio <- risk1 / risk0

# Cox model on the same data: the conditional hazard ratio
cox_hr <- exp(coef(cox_model)["ever_haart"])


G-computation predicts counterfactual outcomes for every person under treatment and under control, then averages the difference. The result is a marginal risk difference, a population-level quantity directly relevant to decision-making, unlike the conditional hazard ratio from the Cox model. Placing the two side by side makes the gap concrete:


Show code
data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Cox hazard ratio (ever vs never HAART)",
    "Risk if everyone initiated HAART, E[Y(1)]",
    "Risk if no one initiated HAART, E[Y(0)]",
    "Marginal risk difference, E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]",
    "Marginal risk ratio, E[Y(1)] / E[Y(0)]"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", cox_hr),
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * risk1),
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * risk0),
    sprintf("%+.1f per 100", 100 * risk_diff),
    sprintf("%.2f", risk_ratio)
  ),
  Scale = c(
    "Conditional, instantaneous rate ratio",
    "Probability", "Probability",
    "Probability difference", "Probability ratio"
  )
) |>
  kable(caption = NULL, align = c("l", "r", "l"))

  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * risk)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +

    "label", x = 1.5, y = max(gcomp_df$risk) * 1.18,
    label = sprintf("Causal risk difference\n%+.1f per 100", 100 * risk_diff),
    size = 3.5, label.size = 0
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.30))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9ecae1", "#3182bd")) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Cumulative mortality risk",
    title = "G-computation reports a marginal, decision-relevant contrast",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "The Cox model on the same data reports only HR = %.2f (a conditional rate ratio, not a risk)",
      cox_hr
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")








Figure 4.1: Two answers to one question, from one dataset. The g-computation bars show the marginal cumulative-mortality risk the population would experience if everyone versus no one initiated HAART; the gap between them is the causal risk difference a clinician can act on. The Cox model fit to the very same data returns only the single hazard ratio in the subtitle, a conditional rate ratio that cannot be read off the risk axis at all.





The Cox model and the logistic g-computation are fitted on the same data, but they answer different questions. The hazard ratio is a conditional, instantaneous rate ratio that does not directly tell us how many deaths would be averted by HAART, and it is non-collapsible: the conditional HR differs from the marginal HR even without confounding. The g-computation risk difference tells you: “X more people per 100 would have died over follow-up if no one had been initiated on HAART compared to if everyone had been.” That is the kind of number patients and clinicians need to make decisions.

4.3.1 Longitudinal failure: treatment-confounder feedback
The point-treatment analysis above already shows that the estimand matters. The HAART setting also illustrates a deeper, structural problem that no choice of point-treatment estimator can fix. In the longitudinal HAART data, CD4 count is measured at each visit and used to guide treatment decisions. But CD4 is also affected by prior treatment: HAART improves CD4 counts. This creates treatment–confounder feedback, a structure where the same variable (CD4) is simultaneously a confounder of future treatment and a consequence of past treatment.
Standard regression faces an impossible choice in this setting. If you do not adjust for time-varying CD4, you leave confounding of future treatment decisions unaddressed. If you do adjust for it, you block part of the causal pathway from HAART through improved CD4 to reduced mortality. Neither approach produces a consistent estimate of the total treatment effect. This is not a matter of choosing the right covariates or the right functional form. It is a structural limitation of the regression framework when applied to longitudinal data with feedback.
The g-methods developed in this handbook (g-computation, IPTW with marginal structural models, and longitudinal TMLE) were designed for exactly this structure. We return to the longitudinal HAART data in the Running Case Study and develop the necessary methods in Part III.
crumbs: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.4 Summary






Key Takeaways




Regression is not inherently causal. It estimates conditional associations under strong model assumptions. An adjusted coefficient is not the same as a causal effect.
Causal inference starts with a question, not a model. Define your causal question and target estimand (e.g., the ATE on the risk difference scale) before choosing an analytic method.
The counterfactual framework clarifies what we want to estimate. Y(1), Y(0), and the ATE give us precise, model-free definitions of causal effects.
G-computation, IPTW, and TMLE estimate marginal causal effects. These methods target the population-level quantity defined by the g-computation formula, rather than relying on regression coefficients that conflate the estimand with the model.
The hazard ratio from Cox regression is not the ATE. Hazard ratios are conditional, instantaneous rate measures that do not directly translate to risk differences. This is perhaps the single most important distinction for epidemiologists moving from traditional regression to causal inference methods.

4.5 What comes next
Now that you understand why regression coefficients are not causal effects, the next chapter introduces the Causal Roadmap: a structured workflow that turns a scientific question into a defensible analysis plan, from question definition through estimation and interpretation.

title: 4  Why We Need a Causal Roadmap
text:
4.6 Check your understanding


Q1. Why can’t you interpret an adjusted logistic regression coefficient as the ATE?

The adjusted coefficient from logistic regression is a conditional log-odds ratio. It describes the association between treatment and outcome within strata defined by the covariates in the model. This differs from the ATE (a marginal risk difference) in at least two ways. First, the odds ratio is non-collapsible: even without confounding, a conditional odds ratio and a marginal odds ratio will differ, so you cannot read the coefficient as a population-level summary. Second, the coefficient li
