section: 17.2 Creating custom learners with different tuning parameters
text:
17.2 Creating custom learners with different tuning parameters
A powerful feature of Super Learner is that you can include multiple versions of the same algorithm with different tuning parameters. Rather than tuning each learner separately, you let the metalearner figure out which version is best.


Show code
# Custom random forest with different mtry values
1SL.ranger.mtry2 <- function(..., mtry = 2) SL.ranger(..., mtry = mtry)
SL.ranger.mtry4 <- function(..., mtry = 4) SL.ranger(..., mtry = mtry)

# Custom LASSO with different alpha (mixing parameter)
2SL.glmnet.ridge <- function(..., alpha = 0)   SL.glmnet(..., alpha = alpha)
SL.glmnet.enet  <- function(..., alpha = 0.5) SL.glmnet(..., alpha = alpha)

# Expanded library
SL_lib_expanded <- c(
  "SL.glm",
  "SL.mean",
  "SL.earth",
  "SL.glmnet",
  "SL.glmnet.ridge",
  "SL.glmnet.enet",
  "SL.ranger",
  "SL.ranger.mtry2",
  "SL.ranger.mtry4"
)

sl_expanded <- SuperLearner(
  Y = Y,
  X = X_df,
  family = binomial(),
  SL.library = SL_lib_expanded,
  method = "method.NNloglik",
  cvControl = list(V = 5L)
)

sl_expanded



1

Wrapper pattern: create named functions that call the base wrapper with a fixed hyperparameter; including multiple versions in the library lets the metalearner select the best mtry without manual tuning

2

alpha = 0 gives ridge regression (all variables kept, coefficients shrunk); alpha = 0.5 gives elastic net (compromise between LASSO sparsity and ridge stability); including both lets the metalearner decide the right regularization type for this dataset





Call:  
SuperLearner(Y = Y, X = X_df, family = binomial(), SL.library = SL_lib_expanded,  
    method = "method.NNloglik", cvControl = list(V = 5L)) 

                         Risk       Coef
SL.glm_All          0.2964437 0.77721316
SL.mean_All         0.3232336 0.04753971
SL.earth_All        0.3073118 0.17524713
SL.glmnet_All       0.2969333 0.00000000
SL.glmnet.ridge_All 0.2963429 0.00000000
SL.glmnet.enet_All  0.2969259 0.00000000
SL.ranger_All       0.3276642 0.00000000
SL.ranger.mtry2_All 0.3254135 0.00000000
SL.ranger.mtry4_All       Inf 0.00000000








Library Design Principles




Start diverse. Include at least one parametric model (GLM), one regularized model (LASSO/elastic net), one tree-based model (random forest or xgboost), and one nonparametric smoother (MARS/earth or GAM).
Include a simple benchmark. Always include SL.mean (intercept-only) and SL.glm. If these get most of the weight, your covariates may not be very predictive.
Vary tuning parameters. Include 2–3 versions of flexible learners with different hyperparameters. This is computationally cheaper than formal grid search and lets the metalearner handle selection.
Including weak learners is generally safe. They receive near-zero weight. In large samples, the penalty for library size is logarithmic in \(K\), but in finite samples, very large libraries can reduce effective sample size for metalearner estimation.

text:
17.3 Using screening wrappers
For high-dimensional data, you can screen variables before fitting a learner. This is especially useful for algorithms that scale poorly with many covariates.


Show code
# Screen top 3 variables by correlation before fitting GLM
screen.corP <- function(Y, X, family, ...) {
  cors <- abs(apply(X, 2, cor, y = Y))
  rank(cors) >= (ncol(X) - 2)
}

# Use list format to pair screener with learner
SL_lib_screen <- list(
  c("SL.glm", "All"),
  c("SL.glm", "screen.corP"),
  c("SL.ranger", "All"),
  c("SL.glmnet", "All")
)

title: 9  Super Learner: Ensemble Machine Learning for Causal Inference
text:
19.1 Simulated treatment–outcome data


Show code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 3000

# Covariates
W_sim <- tibble(
  age    = rnorm(n, 70, 8),
  bmi    = rnorm(n, 27, 4),
  sbp    = rnorm(n, 140, 18),
  smoker = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3),
  cvd    = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.5 + 0.04 * (age - 65) + 0.4 * smoker))
)

# Treatment model (true propensity score), with nonlinear terms
W_sim <- W_sim %>%
  mutate(
    ps_true = plogis(-1.5 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.02 * bmi +
                      0.5 * cvd + 0.3 * smoker +
                      0.01 * (age - 65) * cvd),
    A = rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)
  )

# Outcome model (true), with nonlinear terms
W_sim <- W_sim %>%
  mutate(
    mu1_true = plogis(-2.5 + 0.4 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.03 * bmi +
                       0.6 * cvd + sin(sbp / 40) +
                       0.02 * (age - 65) * cvd),
    mu0_true = plogis(-2.5 +       0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.03 * bmi +
                       0.6 * cvd + sin(sbp / 40) +
                       0.02 * (age - 65) * cvd),
    Y = rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(A == 1, mu1_true, mu0_true))
  )

# True ATE
true_ate <- mean(W_sim$mu1_true - W_sim$mu0_true)
cat("True ATE:", round(true_ate, 4), "\n")

19.3 Generate predictions for TMLE


Show code
logit <- function(p) log(p / (1 - p))
expit <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

# Propensity scores
ps_hat <- predict(g_sl, X_covariates)$pred[, 1]

# Bound propensity scores away from 0 and 1
1ps_hat <- pmin(pmax(ps_hat, 0.01), 0.99)

# Initial outcome predictions at observed A
Q_init <- predict(Q_sl, X_with_A)$pred[, 1]

# Counterfactual predictions: set A = 1 and A = 0 for everyone
X_A1 <- X_with_A; X_A1$A <- 1
X_A0 <- X_with_A; X_A0$A <- 0

Q1_init <- predict(Q_sl, X_A1)$pred[, 1]
Q0_init <- predict(Q_sl, X_A0)$pred[, 1]

# G-computation estimate (before targeting)
gcomp_ate <- mean(Q1_init - Q0_init)
cat("G-computation ATE (SL, before targeting):", round(gcomp_ate, 4), "\n")



1

Truncate propensity scores to \([0.01, 0.99]\) before using them in TMLE or IPTW: scores near 0 or 1 blow up the clever covariate \(H = A/e(W) - (1-A)/(1-e(W))\), destabilizing the fluctuation step. The threshold 0.01 is a common default; tighter bounds (e.g., 0.05) reduce variance at the cost of introducing truncation bias; vary this in a sensitivity analysis.

19.4 TMLE targeting step
This is the same fluctuation step from Chapter 8, now using Super Learner for the initial estimates.


Show code
# Clever covariate
H1 <- 1 / ps_hat
H0 <- -1 / (1 - ps_hat)
H_obs <- ifelse(W_sim$A == 1, H1, H0)

# Observed initial Q at observed A
Q_obs_init <- ifelse(W_sim$A == 1, Q1_init, Q0_init)

# Fluctuation model
1epsilon <- glm(W_sim$Y ~ -1 + offset(logit(Q_obs_init)) + H_obs,
               family = binomial)$coef

# Update counterfactual predictions
2Q1_star <- expit(logit(Q1_init) + epsilon * H1)
Q0_star <- expit(logit(Q0_init) + epsilon * H0)

# TMLE estimate
3tmle_ate <- mean(Q1_star - Q0_star)
cat("TMLE ATE (with SL):", round(tmle_ate, 4), "\n")
cat("True ATE:          ", round(true_ate, 4), "\n")



1

Fluctuation model: the Super Learner predictions Q_obs_init enter as a fixed offset on the logit scale; only the single parameter ε is estimated. A near-zero ε means the SL outcome model was already nearly optimal for the ATE estimand.

2

Apply ε to the counterfactual Q predictions on the logit scale; expit() (the inverse logit) maps back to [0,1]; essential when working with probability outcomes

3

The substitution estimator: average the difference of targeted counterfactual predictions over all observations, giving the population-level ATE

title: 9  Super Learner: Ensemble Machine Learning for Causal Inference
text:
22.1 Check your understanding


Q1. Why does Super Learner use cross-validated predictions rather than in-sample predictions to determine the metalearner weights?

If we used in-sample predictions, a highly flexible learner (like a deep random forest or neural network) could achieve near-perfect training accuracy by memorizing the data. The metalearner would then give it all the weight, and the ensemble would overfit badly. Cross-validated predictions provide an honest assessment of each learner’s generalization performance. A learner that memorizes training data will predict poorly on the held-out fold, and the metalearner will down-weight it accordingly.



Q2. You run Super Learner for a propensity score model and the intercept-only learner (SL.mean) receives the largest weight. What does this suggest?

If the intercept-only learner receives substantial weight, this may reflect weak predictive signal in the covariates, limited sample size, an overly complex library relative to the data, or genuine simplicity in the outcome surface. It does not have a single interpretation. Possible explanations include: (1) treatment really is nearly randomized given your covariates (good news for causal inference), (2) important confounders are missing from your model (dangerous; you may have unmeasured confounding), (3) the covariates need better pre-processing (e.g., you included age as a categorical variable when it should be continuous), or (4) the sample size is too small for flexible learners to outperform the marginal mean. You should investigate which interpretation is correct before proceeding with your causal analysis.



Q3. A colleague argues that you should just use xgboost for the propensity score because “it always wins Kaggle competitions.” How would you respond?

While xgboost is a powerful algorithm, no single learner dominates in all settings. “Winning Kaggle” requires optimizing prediction accuracy for a specific dataset with specific tuning; which is exactly what Super Learner automates. If xgboost truly is the best algorithm for your data, Super Learner will discover this and give it the largest weight. But if your data has a simpler structure where logistic regression or LASSO performs comparably, Super Learner will use those instead (or combine them). Additionally, for causal inference we care about calibrated probabilities, not just ranking accuracy. An out-of-the-box xgboost model optimized for classification accuracy may produce poorly calibrated propensity scores that create extreme IPTW weights. Super Learner with a log-likelihood metalearner directly optimizes calibration.



Q4. In the hand-coded example, we normalized the NNLS weights to sum to 1. Is this necessary? What if they don’t sum to 1?

Normalization is not strictly required by the theory, but it is standard practice. Without normalization, the NNLS weights are the raw coefficients from the constrained regression, and the ensemble predictions may systematically over- or under-predict. Normalizing to sum to 1 makes the ensemble a convex combination of the candidates, which ensures that the ensemble’s predictions stay in the same range as the individual learners’ predictions. For binary outcomes, this helps keep predicted probabilities in \([0, 1]\). The SuperLearner package normalizes by default with method.NNLS.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.1 1. Why the speed of an estimator matters
One estimator flexible enough to fit almost any relationship, yet provably fast enough for valid inference
Estimated reading time: 25 minutes
Super Learner (Chapter 9) gives an honest way to pick the best blend of prediction algorithms, but it leaves one question unanswered. TMLE promises confidence intervals that are valid even when the nuisance models are estimated with machine learning, and that promise comes with fine print: the nuisance estimates have to approach the truth fast enough as the sample grows. Most flexible algorithms, including random forests and gradient boosting, come with no guarantee about how fast their error shrinks. The highly adaptive lasso (HAL) is the unusual exception. It is flexible enough to recover almost any relationship between covariates and outcome, yet it converges quickly enough, under a mild condition, to satisfy the requirement TMLE needs. That combination is why HAL keeps appearing in targeted-learning work, and why it is worth understanding on its own.
A doubly robust estimator such as TMLE combines an outcome model and a propensity model. Its confidence intervals are trustworthy when the product of the two models’ errors vanishes quickly as the sample grows. A useful rule of thumb is that each nuisance estimate should approach the truth faster than the fourth root of the sample size. A simple, correctly specified regression clears this bar easily. The price of that simplicity is the risk of getting the functional form wrong, which biases the estimate in a way no amount of data fixes.
Flexible machine learning protects against the wrong functional form, but most flexible methods come with no guarantee about how fast their error shrinks, so they can quietly violate the rate condition and leave the confidence interval too narrow. There are two ways out. One is to change the estimator so it no longer needs the rate condition, which is what cross-validated TMLE does through sample splitting (Chapter 11). The other is to use a flexible learner that does meet the rate condition. HAL is that learner.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.2 2. What HAL fits
The idea behind HAL is easier to picture than its name suggests. Take every covariate and, at each value it takes in the data, define a simple step that switches from zero to one. Do the same for pairs of covariates, triples, and so on. This produces a very large collection of step-shaped building blocks. Any reasonable relationship between covariates and outcome can be written as a weighted sum of these steps: a smooth curve becomes a staircase with many small steps, a sharp threshold becomes one large step, and an interaction becomes a step that only switches on when two covariates are both above their cutpoints.
HAL fits a weighted sum of all these building blocks at once, using the lasso to keep the total size of the weights under control. The single tuning quantity is that total size, which corresponds to how much the fitted function is allowed to wiggle. A small budget yields a nearly flat fit; a larger budget lets the staircase follow the data more closely. In one sentence, HAL is a lasso over a very large basis of step-function interactions, with one penalty governing flexibility.
Because the building blocks include sharp steps and interactions automatically, HAL captures the kinds of relationships that defeat a main-terms regression. A clinical example: if mortality rises steeply once CD4 falls below roughly 200 cells per microliter, and that threshold matters more in older patients, a main-terms logistic regression will smooth the threshold away and miss the age interaction, while HAL can represent both with a few of its step blocks.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
section: 10.3 3. The one assumption, and the payoff
text:
10.3 3. The one assumption, and the payoff
HAL needs the true relationship to have finite variation, which means it does not wiggle without limit: it can rise, fall, jump, and bend, but only a controlled total amount across the covariate space. For essentially every relationship an epidemiologist would posit between patient characteristics and an outcome, this holds.
Under that mild condition, HAL converges to the truth at a rate faster than the fourth-root bar from Section 1, regardless of how many covariates are involved. That is the payoff: HAL is flexible like machine learning yet fast like a correctly specified parametric model, so it can serve as the nuisance estimator in TMLE and deliver valid confidence intervals, in many settings without requiring sample splitting (Benkeser and Laan 2016; Laan and Rose 2011).

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.4 4. Using HAL in practice
There are two natural ways to use HAL, and the first is the safer default. Add it as one candidate in a Super Learner library (SL.hal9001). The ensemble then leans on HAL where its flexible fit helps and on simpler learners where it does not, and the analyst gets HAL’s strengths without betting the whole analysis on it. The second way is to use HAL directly as the outcome or propensity estimator inside TMLE, which is the route that most cleanly inherits the rate guarantee.
The hal9001 package implements both. The two knobs worth knowing are the maximum interaction order, which sets whether HAL considers single covariates only, pairs, or higher combinations, and the smoothness setting, which controls whether the building blocks are sharp steps or smoother pieces. The main practical cost is computation: the basis grows quickly with the number of covariates and the sample size, so analysts often cap the interaction order at two and screen covariates before fitting in high-dimensional problems.


Show code
source("_data/load-haart-cohort.R")
library(hal9001)

X <- as.matrix(haart_baseline[, c("age", "sex", "cd4_sqrt_baseline")])
Y <- haart_baseline$died

# Fit the outcome model with HAL: pairwise interactions of step-function bases.
hal_fit <- fit_hal(X = X, Y = Y, family = "binomial", max_degree = 2)

# Compare HAL's fitted mortality risks with a main-terms logistic regression.
p_hal <- as.numeric(predict(hal_fit, new_data = X))
p_glm <- predict(glm(died ~ age + sex + cd4_sqrt_baseline,
                     family = binomial, data = haart_baseline), type = "response")

summary(p_hal); summary(p_glm)


    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
0.006777 0.016643 0.020173 0.025833 0.023926 0.232260 


    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
0.006288 0.014061 0.020010 0.025833 0.029918 0.146939

  ggplot(aes(p_glm, p_hal)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Main-terms logistic regression risk", y = "HAL fitted risk",

Where points leave the dashed 45-degree line, HAL has captured structure (CD4 thresholds and age interactions) that the additive logistic model cannot represent; those better nuisance fits are what give TMLE its rate guarantee.





To use HAL inside an ensemble instead, list it as a learner and let Super Learner weight it against the others.

  Y = Y, X = as.data.frame(X), family = binomial(),
  SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean", "SL.hal9001")
)
sl_fit  # the coefficient on SL.hal9001 shows how much weight the ensemble gives HAL

    "SL.mean", "SL.hal9001"))

SL.glm_All     0.02484863 0.6233892
SL.mean_All    0.02519676 0.0000000

Where the true outcome surface has a threshold or interaction, HAL’s fitted risks will separate patients that the main-terms model lumps together, and in a TMLE analysis those better nuisance fits translate into a less biased effect estimate with intervals that keep their nominal coverage.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
section: 10.5 5. Where HAL is the wrong tool, and what it does not fix
text:
10.5 5. Where HAL is the wrong tool, and what it does not fix
HAL is computationally demanding. With many covariates or a large sample, the full basis can exhaust memory, so capping the interaction order and screening covariates first are usually necessary, and at some scale a different learner is simply more practical. The finite-variation assumption, although mild, is still an assumption; a relationship that genuinely behaves erratically across the covariate space is one HAL cannot represent well.
Most importantly, HAL is a better way to estimate nuisance functions, not a way to escape the causal assumptions. It does nothing for unmeasured confounding, and it does not manufacture support where the data have none. If positivity fails, HAL will extrapolate across the gap as silently as any other flexible model (Chapter 12). A faster, more flexible nuisance estimator makes the statistical step more reliable; it leaves the identification step exactly where the Causal Roadmap left it.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.6 Connections to other chapters
HAL is one more candidate for the Super Learner library of Chapter 9, distinguished by the convergence guarantee that the doubly robust estimators of Chapter 8 rely on for valid inference. It offers an alternative to the sample-splitting route of cross-validated TMLE in Chapter 11: where CV-TMLE removes the rate requirement by splitting the data, HAL satisfies it by construction. Both are reasonable defaults, and they can be combined.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.7 Sources and further reading

Benkeser and Laan (2016) introduces the highly adaptive lasso and its convergence-rate guarantee.
Laan and Rose (2011) places HAL within the targeted-learning framework and its inference requirements.
The hal9001 R package implements the estimator: https://cran.r-project.org/package=hal9001.

title: 10  The Highly Adaptive Lasso
text:
10.8 Check your understanding


Q1. Why does TMLE care about how fast a nuisance estimator converges, when ordinary prediction tasks only care about accuracy?

TMLE’s confidence intervals are valid when the combined error of the outcome and propensity models shrinks faster than a set rate (roughly the fourth root of the sample size). If a flexible learner is accurate but converges slowly, the intervals can be too narrow and overstate certainty. A pure prediction task has no such requirement because it is not trying to support a confidence interval for a causal effect.



Q2. In plain terms, what does HAL fit, and what single quantity controls its flexibility?

HAL fits a weighted sum of many simple step-shaped building blocks defined at the observed covariate values and their interactions, so it can represent thresholds, bends, and interactions automatically. The lasso penalty bounds the total size of the weights, which corresponds to how much the fitted function is allowed to wiggle. That single budget is what trades a flat fit against a fit that follows the data closely.



Q3. A reviewer says “you used HAL, so positivity is no longer a concern.” Is that right?

No. HAL improves how well the nuisance functions are estimated, which helps the statistical step, but it does not create data support where there is none. If some covariate group never received one of the treatments, HAL will extrapolate across that gap just like any flexible model. Positivity, like no unmeasured confounding, is an identification assumption that a better estimator cannot repair.







Benkeser, David, and Mark J. van der Laan. 2016. “The Highly Adaptive Lasso Estimator.” In 2016 IEEE International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA), 689–96. https://doi.org/10.1109/DSAA.2016.93.


Laan, Mark J van der, and Sherri Rose. 2011. “Targeted Learning: Causal Inference for Observational and Experimental Data.” Springer.

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
11.1 The Problem That Motivates All Three Variants
Estimated reading time: 30 minutes
Chapter 8 introduced TMLE as a doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient estimator that combines flexible outcome modeling with a targeting step. In many applications, standard TMLE works well. But three practical problems can arise, each addressed by a different TMLE variant:
This chapter explains the non-technical intuition for each, when and why to use it, and how to implement it.
Recall the standard TMLE recipe from Chapter 8:
The asymptotic guarantees of TMLE (consistency, efficiency, valid confidence intervals) depend on regularity conditions for the nuisance estimators \(\hat{Q}\) and \(\hat{g}\). The most important of these is the Donsker condition, which roughly requires that the nuisance estimators do not overfit the data too aggressively.
Each of the three variants addresses a different facet of this problem.
crumbs: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
Initial estimation: Fit an outcome model \(\hat{Q}(A, W)\) and a propensity score \(\hat{g}(W)\), typically using Super Learner.
Targeting step: Update \(\hat{Q}\) along a least-favorable parametric submodel, using \(\hat{g}\) as the “clever covariate.”
Plug in: Compute the causal effect estimate from the updated \(\hat{Q}^*\).








When Standard TMLE Can Fail



Standard TMLE’s theoretical guarantees assume the nuisance estimators fall in a Donsker class, a set of functions with controlled complexity. This is satisfied by parametric models and many regularized estimators, but can be violated by:

Highly adaptive machine learning (deep ensembles, unregularized random forests, neural networks)
Super Learners with very large candidate libraries
High-dimensional settings where the number of covariates grows with sample size

When the Donsker condition fails, the influence-curve-based variance estimator may be anti-conservative, confidence intervals can have below-nominal coverage, and the estimator may not be asymptotically linear.
crumbs: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
11.2 CV-TMLE: Cross-Validated TMLE

11.2.1 The intuition
CV-TMLE (Zheng and Laan 2011, 2010) solves the Donsker problem through sample splitting. The idea is simple: if you fit your nuisance models on one part of the data and evaluate the targeting step on a held-out part, the nuisance estimator is a fixed function when applied to the validation data. Fixed functions are trivially Donsker. This is the same insight that powers cross-validation and, more recently, double/debiased machine learning (DML) (Chernozhukov et al. 2018).
In practice, CV-TMLE uses V-fold cross-validation:

Split the data into V folds.
For each fold \(v\), fit \(\hat{Q}^{(-v)}\) and \(\hat{g}^{(-v)}\) on the training data (all folds except \(v\)).
Generate predictions for fold \(v\) using the models fit without fold \(v\).
Stack all V sets of predictions together.
Run the TMLE targeting step on the full (stacked) dataset using the cross-validated predictions.
Compute the estimate and influence-curve-based inference.

By fitting nuisance models on training data and targeting on validation data, CV-TMLE completely removes the Donsker requirement. You can use arbitrarily complex machine learning—deep Super Learners, HAL, neural networks—without worrying that overfitting will invalidate your inference. The price is a modest increase in computational cost (fitting V models instead of one).


11.2.2 CV-TMLE vs. Double Machine Learning
CV-TMLE and DML (debiased machine learning) both use sample splitting and both achieve semiparametric efficiency. The key difference is the estimator type:








Property
CV-TMLE
DML




Estimator type
Substitution (plug-in)
Estimating equation (one-step)


Respects parameter bounds
Yes (e.g., probabilities stay in [0,1])
Not guaranteed


Targeting step
Updates the outcome model directly
Adds a bias-correction term


Finite-sample behavior
Generally more stable
Can produce out-of-range estimates



In practice, the substitution property of CV-TMLE matters when the outcome is rare (estimated probabilities near 0) or when the treatment effect is small. DML can produce negative probability estimates; CV-TMLE cannot.


11.2.3 When to use CV-TMLE

Always a safe default: CV-TMLE is never worse than standard TMLE asymptotically, and it is strictly better when using aggressive ML. Many practitioners now use CV-TMLE as their default.
Large Super Learner libraries: If your library includes dozens of candidates or highly adaptive algorithms (HAL, deep learners), CV-TMLE is strongly recommended.
High-dimensional covariates: When the number of potential confounders is large relative to sample size.



11.2.4 Implementation in R
The tmle3 package in the tlverse ecosystem implements CV-TMLE natively. The older tmle package does not support cross-validation by default, but you can implement it manually by cross-validating the initial fits.
We use the shared ART cohort throughout, loaded with its canonical variable names (ever_haart = treatment, died = outcome, cd4_sqrt_baseline = baseline CD4) so the same data object can be reused across chapters.


Show code
library(dplyr)
library(SuperLearner)
library(tmle)

source("_data/load-haart-cohort.R")
d <- haart_baseline
W <- d[, c("age", "sex", "cd4_sqrt_baseline")]

SL_lib <- c("SL.glm", "SL.glmnet", "SL.mean")

# --- Standard TMLE (no cross-validation) ---
set.seed(42)
fit_standard <- tmle(
  Y = d$died,
  A = d$ever_haart,
  W = W,
  Q.SL.library = SL_lib,
  g.SL.library = SL_lib,
  family = "binomial"
)

ate_std <- fit_standard$estimates$ATE$psi
ci_std  <- fit_standard$estimates$ATE$CI
cat(sprintf("Standard TMLE ATE: %.4f (95%% CI: %.4f, %.4f)\n",
            ate_std, ci_std[1], ci_std[2]))
#> Standard TMLE ATE: -0.0140 (95% CI: -0.0320, 0.0040)



11.2.4.1 Doubly robust cross-check: TMLE vs. AIPW
TMLE and AIPW (augmented inverse-probability weighting) are both doubly robust and asymptotically equivalent: built from the same nuisance models, they should give nearly identical point estimates. (The AIPW CRAN package is not available in this build, so we compute the AIPW estimator directly from the nuisance fits, which makes the equivalence transparent.)


Show code
A <- d$ever_haart
Y <- d$died

set.seed(42)
g_fit <- SuperLearner(Y = A, X = W, SL.library = SL_lib, family = binomial())
g1 <- pmin(pmax(predict(g_fit, W)$pred[, 1], 0.025), 0.975)  # bounded PS

Q_fit <- SuperLearner(Y = Y, X = data.frame(A = A, W),
                      SL.library = SL_lib, family = binomial())
Q1 <- predict(Q_fit, data.frame(A = 1, W))$pred[, 1]
Q0 <- predict(Q_fit, data.frame(A = 0, W))$pred[, 1]

# AIPW (efficient-influence-function) estimator of E[Y(1)] and E[Y(0)]
psi1 <- mean(A / g1 * (Y - Q1) + Q1)
psi0 <- mean((1 - A) / (1 - g1) * (Y - Q0) + Q0)
ate_aipw <- psi1 - psi0

IC_aipw <- (A / g1) * (Y - Q1) + Q1 - psi1 -
           ((1 - A) / (1 - g1)) * (Y - Q0) - Q0 + psi0
se_aipw <- sqrt(var(IC_aipw) / nrow(d))

cat(sprintf("AIPW ATE:          %.4f (95%% CI: %.4f, %.4f)\n",
            ate_aipw, ate_aipw - 1.96 * se_aipw, ate_aipw + 1.96 * se_aipw))
#> AIPW ATE:          -0.0143 (95% CI: -0.0322, 0.0037)


The two estimates agree to the third decimal place, as expected for two doubly robust estimators sharing the same nuisance models. The practical difference is structural rather than numerical here: TMLE is a substitution estimator, so its estimate is guaranteed to respect the natural bounds of the parameter (a risk difference implied by probabilities in \([0, 1]\)), whereas the AIPW estimating-equation form carries no such guarantee and can stray out of range when the outcome is rare or weights are extreme.


11.2.4.2 Cross-validated targeting: standard TMLE vs. CV-TMLE


Show code
# --- Manual CV-TMLE (3-fold for teaching) ---
# Demonstrates the cross-validation logic explicitly. Production analyses
# should use V = 5 or V = 10; we use V = 3 to keep the chapter fast.
# tmle3 in the tlverse performs this cross-validation automatically.

set.seed(42)
n <- nrow(d)
V <- 3
folds <- sample(rep(1:V, length.out = n))

Qbar_cv <- matrix(NA, n, 2)  # columns: Q(0,W), Q(1,W)
g_cv <- rep(NA, n)

for (v in 1:V) {
  train <- folds != v
  valid <- folds == v

  # Fit outcome model on training data
  Q_fit_v <- SuperLearner(
    Y = d$died[train],
    X = data.frame(A = d$ever_haart[train], W[train, ]),
    SL.library = SL_lib, family = binomial()
  )
  Qbar_cv[valid, 1] <- predict(Q_fit_v, data.frame(A = 0, W[valid, ]))$pred[, 1]
  Qbar_cv[valid, 2] <- predict(Q_fit_v, data.frame(A = 1, W[valid, ]))$pred[, 1]

  # Fit propensity score on training data
  g_fit_v <- SuperLearner(
    Y = d$ever_haart[train], X = W[train, ],
    SL.library = SL_lib, family = binomial()
  )
  g_cv[valid] <- predict(g_fit_v, W[valid, ])$pred[, 1]
}

g_cv <- pmin(pmax(g_cv, 0.025), 0.975)

# --- Targeting step on the full dataset using the CV predictions ---
H1 <- d$ever_haart / g_cv
H0 <- -(1 - d$ever_haart) / (1 - g_cv)

Q_logit_A <- qlogis(ifelse(d$ever_haart == 1, Qbar_cv[, 2], Qbar_cv[, 1]))
eps_fit <- glm(d$died ~ -1 + offset(Q_logit_A) + H1 + H0, family = binomial)
eps <- coef(eps_fit)

Q1_star <- plogis(qlogis(Qbar_cv[, 2]) + eps["H1"] / g_cv)
Q0_star <- plogis(qlogis(Qbar_cv[, 1]) - eps["H0"] / (1 - g_cv))

mu1 <- mean(Q1_star)
mu0 <- mean(Q0_star)
ate_cv <- mu1 - mu0

IC_cv <- (d$ever_haart / g_cv) * (d$died - Q1_star) + Q1_star - mu1 -
         ((1 - d$ever_haart) / (1 - g_cv)) * (d$died - Q0_star) - Q0_star + mu0
se_cv <- sqrt(var(IC_cv) / n)

cat(sprintf("CV-TMLE (manual, %d-fold) ATE: %.4f (95%% CI: %.4f, %.4f)\n",
            V, ate_cv, ate_cv - 1.96 * se_cv, ate_cv + 1.96 * se_cv))
#> CV-TMLE (manual, 3-fold) ATE: -0.0137 (95% CI: -0.0314, 0.0040)


Putting the three estimators side by side shows how little the point estimate moves on this well-behaved cohort—the value of CV-TMLE is not a different number but trustworthy inference when the nuisance models are fit with aggressive machine learning:


Show code
data.frame(
  Estimator = c("Standard TMLE", "AIPW", "CV-TMLE (3-fold)"),
  ATE       = sprintf("%.4f", c(ate_std, ate_aipw, ate_cv)),
  `95% CI`  = c(
    sprintf("(%.4f, %.4f)", ci_std[1], ci_std[2]),
    sprintf("(%.4f, %.4f)", ate_aipw - 1.96 * se_aipw, ate_aipw + 1.96 * se_aipw),
    sprintf("(%.4f, %.4f)", ate_cv - 1.96 * se_cv, ate_cv + 1.96 * se_cv)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r", "c"))




Table 11.1: Three doubly robust estimates of the ATE of ever initiating HAART on mortality in the ART cohort, from the same data and nuisance library. The point estimates are nearly identical; CV-TMLE’s contribution is valid confidence-interval coverage under highly adaptive learners, not a shifted estimate.






Estimator
ATE
95% CI




Standard TMLE

(-0.0320, 0.0040)


AIPW

(-0.0322, 0.0037)


CV-TMLE (3-fold)

Show code
library(ggplot2)
forest_df <- data.frame(
  Estimator = factor(c("Standard TMLE", "AIPW", "CV-TMLE (3-fold)"),
                     levels = c("CV-TMLE (3-fold)", "AIPW", "Standard TMLE")),
  ate = c(ate_std, ate_aipw, ate_cv),
  lo  = c(ci_std[1], ate_aipw - 1.96 * se_aipw, ate_cv - 1.96 * se_cv),
  hi  = c(ci_std[2], ate_aipw + 1.96 * se_aipw, ate_cv + 1.96 * se_cv)
)
ggplot(forest_df, aes(ate, Estimator)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi)) +
  labs(x = "ATE of ever initiating HAART on mortality", y = NULL,
       title = "Three doubly robust estimators, same data") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.1: The three doubly robust estimates with 95% confidence intervals. The point estimates are nearly indistinguishable on this well-behaved cohort; CV-TMLE’s contribution is trustworthy interval coverage under aggressive machine learning, not a shifted estimate.





In the tlverse ecosystem, tmle3 handles CV-TMLE automatically. For the tmle package, you can approximate CV-TMLE by passing pre-computed cross-validated predictions. The manual implementation above shows the core logic: fit on training folds, predict on validation folds, target on the stacked predictions.

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
11.3 C-TMLE: Collaborative TMLE

11.3.1 The intuition
Standard TMLE fits the propensity score \(\hat{g}(W)\) independently of the outcome model \(\hat{Q}(A, W)\). This makes sense from a pure prediction standpoint: the propensity score should predict treatment assignment as well as possible. But from the standpoint of estimating the causal effect, an overly flexible propensity score can be counterproductive.
Here is the key insight: the propensity score enters TMLE only through the clever covariate \(H = A/g(W)\). If \(g(W)\) is very close to 0 or 1 for some patients (near-positivity violations), the clever covariate explodes, and the targeting step becomes unstable—even if the propensity score fits the data beautifully.
C-TMLE (M. J. van der Laan and Gruber 2010) flips the script: instead of fitting \(g\) to predict treatment well, it builds a sequence of increasingly complex propensity score models and selects the one that produces the best outcome model fit for the target parameter. In other words, the propensity score collaborates with the outcome model.






The Collaboration Principle



In standard TMLE, the propensity score and outcome model are fit independently. C-TMLE breaks this independence:

Start with a simple propensity score (e.g., intercept only: \(g(W) = P(A=1)\)).
Build a sequence of increasingly complex models: \(g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_K\).
For each \(g_k\), compute the targeted update \(\hat{Q}^*_k\) and evaluate a cross-validated loss.
Select the \(g_k\) that minimizes the loss for \(\hat{Q}^*_k\).

This is not choosing the propensity score that predicts treatment best. It is choosing the propensity score that, when plugged into the targeting step, produces the best estimate of the outcome under intervention. Variables that improve treatment prediction but destabilize the causal estimate are excluded.




11.3.2 When to use C-TMLE

Near-positivity violations: When some patients have propensity scores very close to 0 or 1, standard TMLE can be unstable. C-TMLE automatically avoids overfitting the propensity score in ways that amplify these near-violations.
High-dimensional propensity score models: When you have hundreds or thousands of potential confounders (e.g., claims databases), C-TMLE can perform variable selection in the propensity score guided by the target estimand.
Practical positivity problems: Even without theoretical violations, small samples or rare treatment patterns can cause practical instability that C-TMLE mitigates.



11.3.3 Scalable C-TMLE
The original greedy C-TMLE algorithm considers adding one variable at a time and evaluates the targeting step at each step. With \(p\) covariates, this is \(O(p^2)\), which is prohibitive for high-dimensional data. Scalable C-TMLE (Ju et al. 2019) uses pre-ordering strategies to reduce complexity to \(O(p)\):

LASSO-C-TMLE: Order covariates by the LASSO regularization path for the propensity score. Evaluate the targeting step at each point along the path.
Univariate pre-ordering: Rank covariates by their univariate association with treatment, then add them in that order.



11.3.4 Implementation in R
The ctmle R package implements both discrete (greedy) and LASSO-based C-TMLE.


Show code
# install.packages("ctmle")
library(ctmle)

# Prepare data (canonical names from the shared loader)
Y <- d$died
A <- d$ever_haart
W_mat <- as.matrix(W)

# --- LASSO-C-TMLE ---
# Step 1: Fit initial outcome model Q(A, W)
Q_init <- SuperLearner(
  Y = Y, X = data.frame(A = A, W_mat),
  SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"), family = binomial()
)
Q0 <- predict(Q_init, newdata = data.frame(A = 0, W_mat))$pred[, 1]
Q1 <- predict(Q_init, newdata = data.frame(A = 1, W_mat))$pred[, 1]
Q_mat <- cbind(QAW = ifelse(A == 1, Q1, Q0), Q0W = Q0, Q1W = Q1)

# Step 2: Get LASSO regularization path for the propensity score
glmnet_fit <- glmnet::glmnet(x = W_mat, y = A, family = "binomial", nlambda = 20)

# Step 3: C-TMLE selects the lambda (propensity score complexity) that
#         produces the best TMLE for the causal estimate
set.seed(42)
fit_ctmle <- ctmleGlmnet(
  Y = as.numeric(Y), A = as.numeric(A),
  W = data.frame(W_mat), Wg = data.frame(W_mat),
  Q = Q_mat,
  lambdas = glmnet_fit$lambda,
  ctmletype = 1,         # forward selection along LASSO path
  family = "binomial",
  V = 5                  # folds for cross-validated selection
)

cat("=== C-TMLE (LASSO path) ===\n")
#> === C-TMLE (LASSO path) ===
cat(sprintf("ATE:  %.4f\n", fit_ctmle$est))
#> ATE:  -0.0095
cat(sprintf("Best lambda index: %d (of %d along path)\n",
    fit_ctmle$best_k, length(glmnet_fit$lambda)))
#> Best lambda index: 1 (of 12 along path)
cat("Compare to standard TMLE above---C-TMLE may differ when\n")
#> Compare to standard TMLE above---C-TMLE may differ when
cat("it selects a simpler propensity score to stabilize estimation.\n")
#> it selects a simpler propensity score to stabilize estimation.


The difference between standard TMLE and C-TMLE is most visible when there are near-positivity violations. In the ART cohort, patients with very low CD4 counts are almost always treated, creating near-violations. C-TMLE automatically finds the propensity score complexity that balances confounding adjustment against instability from extreme weights.

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
11.4 A-TMLE: Adaptive TMLE

11.4.1 The intuition
A-TMLE (M. J. van der Laan et al. 2025; M. van der Laan et al. 2025) addresses a different problem: how to safely borrow strength from external data. Suppose you have a small randomized trial and a large observational database. Can you use the observational data to improve precision without introducing bias?
The challenge is that the observational data may differ from the trial population in unmeasured ways. Naive pooling can introduce bias. Ignoring the external data wastes information.
A-TMLE takes a principled middle path:

Decompose the estimand: Write the ATE as the difference between a “pooled ATE” (using both RCT and external data) and a “bias term” (the effect of being in the RCT on the outcome, conditional on treatment and covariates).
Data-adaptively estimate the bias: Use machine learning to learn a working model for the bias term. If the bias is simple (e.g., explained by measured covariates), large efficiency gains are possible.
Guarantee no harm: By construction, A-TMLE is always at least as efficient as using the RCT data alone. If the external data are badly biased, A-TMLE learns to ignore them.







The “No Harm” Guarantee



A-TMLE’s defining property is that borrowing external data can help but never hurt. The asymptotic variance of the A-TMLE estimator is at most equal to the variance of the TMLE using RCT data alone. This is because the bias working model is selected by cross-validation: if no model improves on the intercept-only model (which corresponds to ignoring external data), the estimator falls back to the RCT-only analysis.
This makes A-TMLE particularly attractive for regulatory settings, where borrowing from external controls must be justified.




11.4.2 When to use A-TMLE

Single-arm trials with external controls: A-TMLE can augment a single-arm trial with a real-world control arm while guaranteeing that the augmentation does not inflate type I error.
Underpowered RCTs: When the trial is too small for adequate precision, external data can help—but only if the bias is manageable.
Hybrid trial designs: More generally, whenever you want to combine experimental and observational data with formal efficiency guarantees.



11.4.3 Software
A-TMLE is a relatively recent development. Implementation is available in the tlverse ecosystem and in custom code accompanying the original publications. As of 2026, no standalone CRAN package exists, but the methodology is described in detail with reproducible code in the original paper.


Show code
# Conceptual pseudocode for A-TMLE
# (Full implementation requires the tlverse ecosystem or custom code)

# 1. Combine RCT and external data
# pooled_data <- rbind(rct_data, external_data)
# pooled_data$S <- c(rep(1, nrow(rct_data)), rep(0, nrow(external_data)))

# 2. Fit nuisance models on pooled data
# Q_pooled <- SuperLearner(Y ~ A + W, data = pooled_data)
# g_pooled <- SuperLearner(A ~ W, data = pooled_data)

# 3. Estimate bias working model: E[Y | A, W, S=1] - E[Y | A, W, S=0]
# Use cross-validation to select the best bias model
# If bias is zero (external data unbiased), maximum precision gain
# If bias is complex, falls back to RCT-only estimate

# 4. Construct A-TMLE estimator
# The targeting step adjusts for both confounding and bias simultaneously

11.5 Putting It All Together: When to Use Which






Decision Guide



Start with CV-TMLE as your default. It is never worse than standard TMLE and provides valid inference with aggressive machine learning. Then consider:








Scenario
Recommended variant
Why




Standard analysis with Super Learner
CV-TMLE
Removes Donsker condition; safe default


Near-positivity violations or extreme weights
C-TMLE
Propensity score guided by outcome model; avoids instability


High-dimensional covariates (100s+)
Scalable C-TMLE (LASSO-C-TMLE)
\(O(p)\) complexity; automatic variable selection in propensity score


Small RCT + large external database
A-TMLE
Data-adaptive borrowing with no-harm guarantee


Simple analysis, parametric models only
Standard TMLE
Donsker condition satisfied by construction; simplest implementation



These variants are not mutually exclusive. CV-C-TMLE (cross-validated collaborative TMLE) combines the sample-splitting of CV-TMLE with the collaborative propensity score selection of C-TMLE.

title: 11  Advanced TMLE: Cross-Validated, Collaborative, and Adaptive
text:
11.7 Check Your Understanding






Questions




CV-TMLE vs. standard TMLE: You are using a Super Learner with 20 candidate algorithms including neural networks and boosted trees. Should you use standard TMLE or CV-TMLE? Why?
C-TMLE intuition: A colleague says “I should always make my propensity score model as flexible as possible to remove confounding bias.” Explain why this can backfire, and how C-TMLE addresses the problem.
CV-TMLE vs. DML: Both CV-TMLE and double machine learning use cross-fitting. What is the key structural difference, and when does it matter?
A-TMLE: You have a 200-patient single-arm trial and a 50,000-patient claims database. Under what conditions would A-TMLE provide large efficiency gains? Under what conditions would it fall back to the trial-only estimate?









Answers






CV-TMLE. With 20 candidates including neural networks and boosted trees, the Super Learner ensemble is highly data-adaptive and likely violates the Donsker condition. Standard TMLE’s influence-curve-based variance estimator may be anti-conservative, leading to confidence intervals that are too narrow. CV-TMLE eliminates this concern by fitting nuisance models on training folds and targeting on validation folds.
A maximally flexible propensity score will fit the data perfectly, but estimated propensity scores near 0 or 1 create enormous clever covariates \(H = A/g(W)\), making the targeting step unstable. The resulting TMLE estimate may have enormous variance even if the propensity score model is “better” in terms of treatment prediction. C-TMLE addresses this by selecting propensity score complexity based on the causal estimate’s performance, not treatment prediction performance. It may choose a simpler propensity score that produces a better-behaved TMLE estimate.
CV-TMLE is a substitution estimator: it updates the outcome model and plugs it in, so estimates always respect natural bounds (e.g., probabilities in [0,1]). DML is an estimating equation estimator: it adds a bias-correction term to a plug-in estimate, which can produce values outside the parameter space. This matters most when outcomes are rare (probabilities near 0), when sample sizes are small, or when the treatment effect is bounded.
Large gains: When the observational data come from a population similar to the trial, with the same treatment-outcome relationship conditional on measured covariates (i.e., the bias term is small or zero). In the extreme, if the external data are unbiased, A-TMLE effectively adds 50,000 controls to the 200-patient trial. Falls back: When the observational data have large, complex unmeasured confounding that cannot be captured by the bias working model. A-TMLE’s cross-validated model selection will find that no bias model improves on the intercept (which corresponds to ignoring external data), and the estimator reduces to the trial-only analysis.

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
12.1 A cautionary tale from pharmacoepidemiology
Estimated reading time: 50 minutes
A research team set out to estimate the effect of HAART initiation on mortality in an HIV cohort. They carefully assembled a claims-derived dataset, adjusted for dozens of confounders, and ran an IPTW analysis. The result was startling: a risk ratio of 0.12 for mortality, implying HAART cut the death rate by 88%. Clinicians welcomed the magnitude but treatment epidemiologists were skeptical. When the analysts inspected the propensity score distribution they discovered the problem. Patients with very low CD4 counts and recent opportunistic infections were essentially always started on HAART under the guidelines in force at the time, while a small number who never initiated despite meeting those criteria looked nothing like anyone else in the cohort. Those untreated, very-low-CD4 patients had near-zero propensity scores for “no HAART,” and their inverse-probability weights were enormous. A handful of them dominated the entire estimate.
The culprit was a positivity violation: the data contained patient profiles for which one treatment was never (or almost never) observed. No amount of clever modeling can conjure information that the data simply do not contain.
We touched on positivity briefly in Chapter 5 and saw weight instability in Chapter 7. But positivity is too important, and too commonly the root cause of failed causal analyses, to scatter across chapters. This chapter gives it the dedicated treatment it deserves.

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
Learning objectives



After completing this chapter you will be able to:

State the positivity assumption formally and intuitively.
Distinguish structural from practical positivity violations.
Diagnose positivity problems using propensity score plots, overlap statistics, and effective sample size.
Explain how positivity violations distort IPTW, G-computation, and TMLE.
Apply practical remedies including population restriction, weight truncation, and modified treatment policies.

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
13.1 Intuition first
Imagine you want to estimate the causal effect of a drug versus no drug across all patients in your study. Positivity says: for every type of patient defined by the confounders you adjust for, both treatment options must be possible. If some patient profiles always receive the drug (or never receive it), you have no observed counterfactual for that stratum, and the causal contrast there is unidentifiable from data alone. You cannot learn the effect of a treatment in patients who would never have received it, any more than you can politically poll the views of people who never pick up the phone.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
13.2 Formal definition
For every level of confounders \(w\) that occurs in the population (that is, \(P(W = w) > 0\)), we require (Hernán and Robins 2025; Petersen and Laan 2014):
\[
0 < P(A = a \mid W = w) < 1 \quad \text{for all treatment levels } a
\] {#eq-positivity}
In words: the probability of receiving each treatment value, conditional on covariates, is bounded away from zero and one.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
13.3 Connection to identification
Recall the G-computation identification formula from Chapter 5:
\[
\psi = E_W\!\Big[\,E[Y \mid A=1, W] - E[Y \mid A=0, W]\,\Big]
\]
This formula requires us to estimate \(E[Y \mid A=a, W=w]\) for both values of \(a\) at every \(w\) in the population. If \(P(A=1 \mid W=w) = 0\) for some \(w\), we have no treated patients at that covariate value and must extrapolate from other regions. That extrapolation is unverifiable; we are guessing.
By analogy, positivity is like having a restaurant review for every item on the menu. If nobody has ever ordered the fish, you cannot credibly claim it is better or worse than the chicken. You can speculate, but the data are silent on that comparison.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
section: 13.4 Positivity with continuous or high-dimensional covariates
text:
13.4 Positivity with continuous or high-dimensional covariates
The formal definition above is stated for discrete \(W\), where we require \(P(A = a \mid W = w) > 0\) at every support point. When \(W\) is continuous or high-dimensional, the condition generalizes to positivity almost surely: the propensity score \(g(W) = P(A = 1 \mid W)\) must be bounded away from 0 and 1 with probability one in the analysis population.
Practical restatement. There exist constants \(0 < \delta_L \leq \delta_U < 1\) such that \(\delta_L \leq g(W) \leq \delta_U\) almost surely. In applied work, this means the estimated propensity scores should be bounded away from the boundaries, not just on average, but for every observation that contributes to the analysis.
When propensity scores approach 0 or 1 for a non-negligible fraction of the sample, the effective sample size shrinks, influence-function-based variance estimates grow, and the causal estimand becomes poorly identified in the tails of the covariate distribution. For instance, if elderly patients with renal impairment are almost never prescribed the new drug, the propensity score for that group approaches zero, and estimates for their subgroup rely entirely on model extrapolation.
This is not merely a technical annoyance. When positivity fails for a subpopulation, the most principled response is often to revise the estimand rather than to truncate weights or extrapolate. Modified treatment policies and stochastic interventions (see Chapter 16) define interventions that remain within the observed data support by construction, avoiding the need to estimate treatment effects in regions where the data are sparse.
Alternatively, one can restrict the target population to the subset with adequate overlap, acknowledging that the resulting estimate answers a different (but well-defined) causal question. This often arises in claims-based studies when certain comorbidity profiles are strongly associated with one treatment, leaving little or no overlap for the alternative.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
14.1 Structural violations
A structural violation occurs when certain patients cannot receive a treatment by definition or by design.







Example
Why structural




Comparing hysterectomy vs. watchful waiting: men cannot receive hysterectomy
Biological impossibility


Pediatric drug not approved for adults
Regulatory prohibition


Dialysis only available at certain facilities
Geographic/logistic constraint



Because the treatment is truly impossible, you should redefine the target population to exclude those strata. Trying to estimate a causal effect for patients who could never be treated is asking a question the world cannot answer, not just a question the data cannot answer.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
14.2 Practical violations
A practical (or random) violation occurs when treatment is theoretically possible but so rare that the data contain few or no treated (or untreated) patients in certain strata.







Example
Why practical




Very elderly patients rarely prescribed a newer drug
Clinical preference, not prohibition


Patients with severe liver disease rarely enrolled in trials
Selection bias, not impossibility


Patients at small rural sites rarely receive complex interventions
Resource constraints



Practical violations are more insidious because they can be hard to detect. The treatment is not forbidden; it just almost never happens. Analysts may not realize they are forcing the estimator to extrapolate.






Adjusting for more confounders can make positivity worse



Adding covariates reduces confounding bias (good) but splits the data into finer strata, each with fewer patients (bad for positivity). There is a genuine tension between exchangeability and positivity. Targeted Learning methods help manage this trade-off, but they cannot eliminate it.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
section: 15.1 Simulate data with a positivity gap
text:
15.1 Simulate data with a positivity gap


Show code
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)
n <- 2000

# Generate confounders
age <- rnorm(n, mean = 60, sd = 12)
severity <- rbinom(n, 1, prob = 0.4)

# Treatment assignment: strongly depends on age and severity
# Patients with age > 75 AND severity == 1 almost never get treated
logit_ps <- 0.5 - 0.06 * age - 1.8 * severity - 0.04 * (age > 75) * severity * 10
ps_true <- plogis(logit_ps)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, prob = ps_true)

# Outcome (binary: adverse event within 1 year)
lp_y <- -3 + 0.03 * age + 0.8 * severity - 0.5 * A + 0.01 * A * age
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_y))

dat <- tibble(age, severity, A, Y, ps_true)

# Examine the positivity gap
dat |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age <= 55 ~ "<=55",
    age <= 65 ~ "56-65",
    age <= 75 ~ "66-75",
    TRUE       ~ ">75"
  )) |>
  group_by(age_group, severity) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_treated = sum(A),
    prop_treated = mean(A),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(age_group, severity) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Treatment prevalence by age group and severity")

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
15.2 Propensity score density plots
The single most useful positivity diagnostic is a density plot of the estimated propensity score, separated by treatment group.


Show code
# Fit a propensity score model
ps_model <- glm(A ~ age * severity + I(age^2), data = dat, family = binomial)
dat$ps_hat <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

ggplot(dat, aes(x = ps_hat, fill = factor(A))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "#E69F00", "1" = "#56B4E9"),
    labels = c("Untreated", "Treated")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Estimated propensity score",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Group",
    title = "Propensity score overlap plot",
    subtitle = "Poor overlap visible in the left tail (treated patients with very low PS)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 15.1: Propensity score distributions by treatment group in the simulated data. Good overlap (both groups spanning the full range) supports positivity; mass piling up near 0 or 1 in only one group signals near-violations.





Good overlap looks like the two densities sitting on top of each other across most of the propensity score range. Bad overlap looks like one group having density where the other does not. The non-overlapping region is where positivity is violated.

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
15.5 A reusable data-support report
The individual checks above are easier to use as one routine that returns the numbers most worth seeing before trusting any weighted or standardized estimate. Pass the treatment, the estimated propensity score, and a covariate frame; the report gives the propensity mass in the tails, the largest stabilized weight, the effective sample size, and the covariate balance before and after weighting. Later chapters refer back to this report rather than re-deriving the pieces.


Show code
data_support_report <- function(A, ps, W) {
  w   <- ifelse(A == 1, mean(A) / ps, mean(1 - A) / (1 - ps))   # stabilized weights
  ess <- sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2)
  smd <- sapply(W, function(x) {
    s  <- sqrt((var(x[A == 1]) + var(x[A == 0])) / 2)           # pooled SD
    c(before = (mean(x[A == 1]) - mean(x[A == 0])) / s,
      after  = (weighted.mean(x[A == 1], w[A == 1]) -
                weighted.mean(x[A == 0], w[A == 0])) / s)
  })
  list(
    pct_ps_below_05  = round(100 * mean(ps < 0.05), 1),
    pct_ps_above_95  = round(100 * mean(ps > 0.95), 1),
    max_stab_weight  = round(max(w), 1),
    effective_n      = round(ess),
    nominal_n        = length(A),
    smd_before_after = round(t(smd), 3)
  )
}

data_support_report(dat$A, dat$ps_hat, dat[, c("age", "severity")])

age      -0.795 0.237

Read it as a checklist. Any appreciable mass with a propensity below 0.05 or above 0.95 flags patients with little counterfactual support. A maximum stabilized weight in the tens or hundreds, or an effective sample size far below the nominal count, means a few patients dominate. The standardized mean differences should shrink toward zero after weighting; a covariate whose imbalance persists is one the weights failed to balance, which points back to the propensity model. The covariate-by-treatment cell table above complements this by exposing exact structural zeros, and the per-stratum version of the same positivity check, applied inside each subgroup, appears in Chapter 21.

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
16.1 IPTW: extreme weights
IPTW inverts the propensity score, so patients with \(P(A=1 \mid W) \approx 0\) who nonetheless received treatment get enormous weights.


Show code
# Compute IPTW weights
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    ipw = if_else(A == 1, 1 / ps_hat, 1 / (1 - ps_hat))
  )

# Inspect weight distribution
dat |>
  summarise(
    mean_wt   = mean(ipw),
    max_wt    = max(ipw),
    pct_gt_10 = mean(ipw > 10) * 100,
    pct_gt_20 = mean(ipw > 20) * 100
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "IPW weight summary: large weights signal trouble")



IPW weight summary: large weights signal trouble


mean_wt
max_wt
pct_gt_10
pct_gt_20




2.08
488.86
2.45
1.25





Show code
# IPTW estimate (Horvitz-Thompson style)
ate_iptw <- dat |>
  summarise(
    ate = weighted.mean(Y[A == 1], ipw[A == 1]) -
          weighted.mean(Y[A == 0], ipw[A == 0])
  ) |>
  pull(ate)

cat("IPTW ATE estimate:", round(ate_iptw, 3), "\n")


IPTW ATE estimate: -0.046 








Why extreme weights are dangerous



A single patient with a weight of 50 counts as much as 50 patients. If that patient has an unusual outcome (by chance), it can shift the entire ATE estimate. This is not bias in the usual sense; it is finite-sample instability driven by near-violations of positivity.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
16.2 G-computation: silent extrapolation
G-computation fits an outcome model \(E[Y \mid A, W]\) and then predicts under each treatment value for every patient. When positivity is violated, those predictions require the outcome model to extrapolate into covariate regions with no (or very few) treated patients.


Show code
out_model <- lm(Y ~ A * age * severity, data = dat)

dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    Y1_hat = predict(out_model, newdata = mutate(dat, A = 1)),
    Y0_hat = predict(out_model, newdata = mutate(dat, A = 0))
  )

ate_gcomp <- mean(dat$Y1_hat - dat$Y0_hat)
cat("G-computation ATE estimate:", round(ate_gcomp, 3), "\n")


G-computation ATE estimate: -0.029 


G-computation may look stable, but that stability is an illusion. It relies entirely on the parametric model being correct in the extrapolation region, and there is no data to check it. The model might predict that an 90-year-old with severe comorbidities would benefit from treatment, but if no such patient was ever treated, that prediction is pure speculation dressed up as an estimate.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
16.3 TMLE: clever covariate instability
TMLE (Chapter 8, doubly-robust-tmle.qmd) updates the initial outcome model using a “clever covariate” \(H(A, W) = A / g(W) - (1-A) / (1 - g(W))\). When \(g(W)\) is near zero, this clever covariate explodes, just like the IPW weight. TMLE inherits the instability of IPTW through its targeting step, even though it also uses an outcome model. In practice, you might see one or two observations with clever-covariate values ten times larger than the rest, suggesting those patients are driving the entire estimate.


Show code
# Demonstrate clever covariate magnitude
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    clever_cov = A / ps_hat - (1 - A) / (1 - ps_hat)
  )

dat |>
  summarise(
    max_abs_H  = max(abs(clever_cov)),
    q99_abs_H  = quantile(abs(clever_cov), 0.99),
    mean_abs_H = mean(abs(clever_cov))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               caption = "Clever covariate magnitude: large values indicate positivity trouble")



Clever covariate magnitude: large values indicate positivity trouble


max_abs_H
q99_abs_H
mean_abs_H




488.86
22.43
2.08





The bottom line is that no estimator is immune to positivity violations. IPTW shows the problem as weight instability. G-computation hides it behind model extrapolation. TMLE sits in between, inheriting instability through the clever covariate while gaining some protection from the outcome model. The real solution is not to choose a “better” estimator; it is to address the positivity problem directly.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
17.1 Redefine the target population
The most principled response is to restrict the analysis to the population where overlap exists. You are changing the question, not patching the estimator.


Show code
# Restrict to the overlap region (e.g., PS between 0.05 and 0.95)
dat_trimmed <- dat |>
  filter(ps_hat > 0.05, ps_hat < 0.95)

cat("Original sample:", nrow(dat), "\n")


Original sample: 2000 


Show code
cat("After trimming: ", nrow(dat_trimmed),
    sprintf("(%.0f%% retained)\n", 100 * nrow(dat_trimmed) / nrow(dat)))


After trimming:  485 (24% retained)


This is honest. You are now estimating the ATE for the sub-population with adequate support, not the full population. Report this clearly.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
17.2 Weight truncation with sensitivity analysis
If trimming the population is not desirable, you can truncate (cap) the IPW weights at a threshold. This introduces some bias but reduces variance. The key is to try several thresholds and see how the estimate changes.


Show code
truncation_sensitivity <- function(data, thresholds) {
  map_dfr(thresholds, function(thr) {
    d <- data |>
      mutate(ipw_trunc = pmin(ipw, thr))
    ate <- d |>
      summarise(
        ate = weighted.mean(Y[A == 1], ipw_trunc[A == 1]) -
              weighted.mean(Y[A == 0], ipw_trunc[A == 0])
      ) |>
      pull(ate)
    tibble(threshold = thr, ate_estimate = ate, max_weight = thr)
  })
}

thresholds <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, Inf)
results <- truncation_sensitivity(dat, thresholds)

results |>
  mutate(threshold = if_else(is.infinite(threshold), "None", as.character(threshold))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Sensitivity of IPTW to weight truncation")

ggplot(results_plot, aes(x = threshold, y = ate_estimate)) +

    subtitle = "Stable estimates across thresholds suggest robust findings"
  ) +

Figure 17.1: ATE estimate as a function of the propensity-score truncation threshold. A stable line indicates the estimate does not hinge on a handful of extreme weights; a steep slope flags a result driven by near-positivity violations.





If the ATE estimate barely changes as you relax the truncation threshold, the result is not driven by extreme weights and positivity violations are not dominating. If the estimate swings wildly, the causal conclusion depends heavily on a few patients with near-zero propensity scores, and you should be cautious.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
17.3 Modified treatment policies (shift interventions)
Instead of asking “What if everyone received treatment?”, you can ask “What if everyone’s probability of treatment were shifted slightly upward?” This avoids counterfactual scenarios that violate positivity. We will encounter these in detail in later chapters; for now, just note the idea: if the static intervention \(\text{do}(A=1)\) creates positivity problems, a stochastic or shift intervention may not.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
17.4 A remedies decision guide
The responses above are not a menu to pick from at random; the diagnosis points to the remedy. The table maps what the diagnostics show to what to do, and to how the estimand changes as a result.








What the diagnostics show
Recommended response
Estimand consequence




A few extreme weights, estimate stable under truncation
Truncate and report a truncation sensitivity curve
Mild; the target is essentially unchanged


A region of covariate space with no overlap
Restrict to the overlap region
The target becomes the ATE in the overlap population


The question is about the treated, and controls are sparse
Target the ATT rather than the ATE
The question narrows to the treated


A static “treat everyone” regime has no support
Switch to a stochastic or modified treatment policy (Chapter 16, Chapter 20)
The target becomes a feasible, support-respecting intervention


A longitudinal regime loses support across visits
Use a feasible shift rule rather than a fixed path
As above, defined visit by visit



The unifying principle is that a positivity problem signals that the data cannot answer the original question. The honest move is to answer a nearby question the data can support, and to state plainly which question that is.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
17.5 Honest reporting
When positivity problems remain after reasonable adjustments, the most important response is transparency. Report:

The proportion of patients in low-overlap regions.
The maximum and 99th-percentile IPW weights.
The effective sample size (next section).
Sensitivity analyses under different truncation levels.
The sub-populations where the estimate is well supported versus extrapolated.
crumbs: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support

title: 12  Positivity, Overlap, and Data Support
text:
18.3 Threshold guidance
There is no universal cutoff, but common recommendations include:

ESS < 50% of actual sample size: warning flag; inspect weights.
ESS < 20% of actual sample size: serious concern; consider trimming or population restriction.
ESS < n for one group but not the other: asymmetric positivity, often indicating that one treatment direction has poor support.







ESS is a summary, not a diagnosis



A healthy ESS does not guarantee that positivity holds everywhere. A few problematic strata can be masked by many well-behaved ones. Always pair ESS with the overlap plots and covariate-specific tables shown in Chapter 15.
