title: 28  In development
text:
29 Integrating Randomized and Real-World Data
Estimated reading time: 40 minutes
This chapter is a tutorial companion to the methodological papers by Dang et al. (2022) and van der Laan, Qiu, and van der Laan (2024). The methods are implemented in the EScvtmle and atmle R packages. Code examples use simulated data with known ground truth; real applications require careful attention to the identification assumptions discussed below.

title: 28  In development
text:
29.1 Why This Chapter Matters
Chapter 28 introduced the conceptual framework for combining randomized and observational data. This chapter provides the practical implementation, walking through two state-of-the-art TMLE-based methods for data fusion: ES-CV-TMLE (Experiment-Selector Cross-Validated TMLE) and A-TMLE (Adaptive TMLE).
The promise of data fusion is simple: a small RCT provides internal validity (unbiased treatment effect estimation), while a large observational dataset provides statistical power (more patients, narrower confidence intervals). If we could safely combine them, we would get the best of both worlds: unbiased estimates with the precision of a much larger study.
The danger is equally simple: if the observational data are biased (due to unmeasured confounding, different standard of care, or population differences), naive pooling imports that bias into the estimate and can produce confidently wrong conclusions. The target estimand throughout is the treatment effect in the trial-eligible population, estimated with improved precision by borrowing information from the external data.
The two methods in this chapter address this danger in complementary ways:

ES-CV-TMLE (Dang et al. 2022) uses cross-validation to decide whether to pool at all, selecting the experiment (RCT-only vs. RCT+RWD) that minimizes an estimated bias-squared-plus-variance criterion.
A-TMLE (Laan et al. 2025) directly estimates and corrects the bias from pooling, using the highly adaptive lasso to learn the bias structure without pre-specifying its functional form.

Both methods build on the TMLE framework from Chapter 8 and the Super Learner machinery from Chapter 9.

title: 28  In development
text:
30.1 A motivating scenario
Suppose you have a small RCT of 400 patients comparing a new diabetes drug to standard of care, with a composite cardiovascular event (MACE) as the primary endpoint. The RCT alone yields a risk difference of \(-0.7\%\) with a wide 95% CI of \([-2.0\%, 0.5\%]\), not statistically significant.
You also have access to a large claims database (e.g., Optum) with 14,000 patients on the same two treatments. Naive pooling (simply combining the datasets and running TMLE on the merged data) might yield a tighter CI. But the claims data has unmeasured confounders: patients who received the new drug may have been healthier, more adherent, or under closer monitoring. If these unmeasured factors differ between treatment groups, the observational treatment effect is biased.
The naive pooled estimate might be \(-2.5\%\) with a tight CI of \([-3.5\%, -1.5\%]\), statistically significant, but wrong. The narrow CI gives false confidence in a biased estimate.

title: 28  In development
text:
30.2 Formalizing the bias
Let \(S\) denote the study indicator (\(S = 1\) for RCT, \(S = 0\) for RWD), \(A\) the treatment, \(Y\) the outcome, and \(W\) baseline covariates. The pooled-ATE estimand is:
\[
\tilde{\Psi}(P_0) = E\big[E(Y \mid W, A = 1) - E(Y \mid W, A = 0)\big]
\]
This pools the outcome regression across both studies. When the conditional mean outcome differs between studies (\(E(Y_a \mid S = 1, W) \neq E(Y_a \mid W)\)), the pooled-ATE is biased for the true treatment effect.
The RCT-ATE estimand uses only the trial’s outcome model but marginalizes over the broader covariate distribution:
\[
\Psi(P_0) = E_W\big[E(Y \mid S = 1, W, A = 1) - E(Y \mid S = 1, W, A = 0)\big]
\]
The bias is the difference:
\[
\Psi^{\#}(P_0) = \tilde{\Psi}(P_0) - \Psi(P_0)
\]
Both ES-CV-TMLE and A-TMLE target the RCT-ATE \(\Psi(P_0)\), either by detecting when \(\Psi^{\#}\) is large enough to reject the external data (ES-CV-TMLE) or by directly estimating and subtracting \(\Psi^{\#}\) (A-TMLE).

title: 28  In development
text:
34.1 How it works
ES-CV-TMLE uses V-fold cross-validation to decide whether pooling helps or hurts (Dang et al. 2022). The algorithm proceeds as follows:

Split the combined (RCT + RWD) dataset into V cross-validation folds.
In each training fold, fit outcome regressions, treatment mechanisms, and study enrollment models. Compute the ATE under two “experiments”: (a) RCT data only, (b) RCT + RWD pooled.
Evaluate a selection criterion for each experiment: estimated bias\(^2\) + variance. The bias is estimated from the discrepancy between the RCT-only and pooled outcome models. Optionally, a negative control outcome (NCO) can sharpen the bias estimate.
Select the experiment that minimizes the criterion in each fold.
In the validation fold, estimate the ATE using TMLE for the selected experiment.
Average across validation folds to produce the final estimate and confidence interval.

The cross-validation is critical: it prevents the selection from overfitting to the training data. The proportion of folds that select pooling provides a useful diagnostic: if most folds select RCT-only, the external data are likely biased.

title: 28  In development
text:
34.2 Application: WASH Benefits example
The EScvtmle package includes data from the WASH Benefits Bangladesh trial, which studied the effect of sanitation interventions on child growth (length-for-age Z-scores). The dataset includes:

Study 1 (\(S = 1\)): A random sample of 300 observations from the RCT (150 sanitation, 150 control)
Study 2 (\(S = 0\), unbiased): Another random sample of 300 from the remaining RCT data, used as an unbiased external dataset
Study 3 (\(S = 0\), biased): An observational sample where “treatment” is having an improved latrine at baseline, likely confounded by socioeconomic status

This setup lets us test ES-CV-TMLE under both unbiased and biased external data.

34.2.1 Unbiased external data


Show code
library(EScvtmle)

data(wash)

# Use studies 1 (RCT) and 2 (unbiased external)
dat_unbiased <- wash[wash$study %in% c(1, 2), ]
dat_unbiased$study[dat_unbiased$study == 2] <- 0

set.seed(2026)
results_unbiased <- ES.cvtmle(
  txinrwd = TRUE,
  data = dat_unbiased,
  study = "study",
  covariates = c("aged", "sex", "momedu", "hfiacat"),
  treatment_var = "intervention",
  treatment = 1,
  outcome = "laz",
  NCO = "Nlt18scale",
  pRCT = 0.5,
  V = 10,
  Q.SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"),
  g.SL.library = c("SL.glm"),
  Q.discreteSL = TRUE,
  g.discreteSL = TRUE,
  family = "gaussian",
  family_nco = "gaussian",
  fluctuation = "logistic",
  comparisons = list(c(1), c(1, 0)),
  adjustnco = FALSE,
  target.gwt = TRUE
)

# Results
print(results_unbiased)


Key arguments:

txinrwd = TRUE: The active treatment is available in the external data.
comparisons = list(c(1), c(1, 0)): Compare two experiments: RCT only (\(S = 1\)) vs. RCT + RWD (\(S \in \{1, 0\}\)).
NCO = "Nlt18scale": Negative control outcome (household members \(\leq 18\)), which should not be affected by sanitation intervention.
V = 10: 10-fold cross-validation.

With unbiased external data, we expect most folds to select pooling, producing a narrower CI than RCT-only.


34.2.2 Biased external data


Show code
# Use studies 1 (RCT) and 3 (biased external)
dat_biased <- wash[wash$study %in% c(1, 3), ]
dat_biased$study[dat_biased$study == 3] <- 0

set.seed(2026)
results_biased <- ES.cvtmle(
  txinrwd = TRUE,
  data = dat_biased,
  study = "study",
  covariates = c("aged", "sex", "momedu", "hfiacat"),
  treatment_var = "intervention",
  treatment = 1,
  outcome = "laz",
  NCO = "Nlt18scale",
  pRCT = 0.5,
  V = 10,
  Q.SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.mean"),
  g.SL.library = c("SL.glm"),
  Q.discreteSL = TRUE,
  g.discreteSL = TRUE,
  family = "gaussian",
  family_nco = "gaussian",
  fluctuation = "logistic",
  comparisons = list(c(1), c(1, 0)),
  adjustnco = TRUE,
  target.gwt = TRUE
)

print(results_biased)


With biased external data, we expect most folds to select RCT-only. The adjustnco = TRUE flag incorporates the negative control outcome into the bias estimate, which can improve the method’s ability to detect bias.


34.2.3 Interpreting ES-CV-TMLE output
The output includes:

ATE: Point estimates under the bias\(^2\)+variance selector (b2v) and the NCO-adjusted selector (ncobias).
CI: 95% confidence intervals.
proportionselected: The fraction of cross-validation folds that selected each experiment. A high proportion selecting RCT-only signals that the external data are likely biased.
g: Propensity score values; check for near-zero values indicating positivity violations.

title: 28  In development
text:
35.1 How it works
A-TMLE takes a different approach: instead of deciding whether to pool, it always pools but adaptively estimates and corrects the bias (van der Laan, Qiu, and van der Laan 2024). The key innovation is that efficiency gains depend on the complexity of the bias, not just its magnitude.
The algorithm:

Estimate the pooled-ATE \(\tilde{\Psi}\) using standard TMLE on the combined RCT + RWD data.
Estimate the bias \(\Psi^{\#}\) using a flexible working model. A-TMLE uses the highly adaptive lasso (HAL) to learn the bias structure data-adaptively, without pre-specifying its functional form.
Correct: The final estimate is \(\hat{\Psi} = \hat{\tilde{\Psi}} - \hat{\Psi}^{\#}\).

The targeting step ensures the final estimator solves the efficient influence function equation, providing valid inference under appropriate regularity conditions regardless of whether the bias working model is correctly specified.
Why HAL? The highly adaptive lasso can approximate any cadlag function, so it can capture complex bias patterns (interactions, nonlinearities) without the analyst having to specify them. If the bias is zero, HAL shrinks \(\hat{\Psi}^{\#}\) toward zero, and the estimator achieves the efficiency of pooling. If the bias is large, \(\hat{\Psi}^{\#}\) captures it, and the estimator falls back toward the RCT-only estimate.

title: 28  In development
text:
35.2 Application: Simulated RCT + RWD
The atmle package includes a sample dataset for demonstration:


Show code
library(atmle)
library(sl3)

# Load built-in sample data
data(sample_data)

# Define Super Learner library
sl_lib <- list(
  Lrnr_glm$new(),
  Lrnr_xgboost$new()
)

# Standard (non-adaptive) TMLE for comparison
set.seed(2026)
tmle_res <- nonparametric(
  data = mydata,
  S = "S",
  W = c("W1", "W2", "W3", "W4"),
  A = "A",
  Y = "Y",
  family = "gaussian",
  Pi_method = sl_lib,
  g_method = "glm",
  Q_method = sl_lib,
  Q_pooling = TRUE,
  v_folds = 5
)

# A-TMLE with HAL-based bias correction
set.seed(2026)
atmle_res <- atmle(
  data = mydata,
  S = "S",
  W = c("W1", "W2", "W3", "W4"),
  A = "A",
  Y = "Y",
  family = "gaussian",
  theta_method = sl_lib,
  Pi_method = sl_lib,
  g_method = sl_lib,
  theta_tilde_method = sl_lib,
  bias_working_model = "HAL",
  pooled_working_model = "HAL",
  enumerate_basis_args = list(
    max_degree = 3,
    smoothness_orders = 1
  ),
  v_folds = 5
)


Key arguments:

S = "S": Study indicator (1 = RCT, 0 = RWD).
theta_method, Pi_method, g_method, theta_tilde_method: Super Learner libraries for the outcome regression, study enrollment score, treatment mechanism, and marginal outcome, respectively.
bias_working_model = "HAL": Use the highly adaptive lasso to learn the bias structure.
enumerate_basis_args: Control the complexity of the HAL basis functions (higher max_degree allows more complex bias patterns).


35.2.1 Comparing results


Show code
# Compare standard TMLE vs A-TMLE
cat("Standard TMLE (pooled, no bias correction):\n")
cat("  Estimate:", round(tmle_res$psi_pooled_W, 4), "\n")
cat("  95% CI: [", round(tmle_res$lower_pooled_W, 4), ",",
    round(tmle_res$upper_pooled_W, 4), "]\n\n")

cat("A-TMLE (bias-corrected):\n")
cat("  Pooled-ATE estimate:", round(atmle_res$psi_tilde_est, 4), "\n")
cat("  Estimated bias:", round(atmle_res$psi_pound_est, 4), "\n")
cat("  Corrected estimate:", round(atmle_res$est, 4), "\n")
cat("  95% CI: [", round(atmle_res$lower, 4), ",",
    round(atmle_res$upper, 4), "]\n")




35.2.2 Interpreting A-TMLE output

est: The bias-corrected ATE estimate \(\hat{\Psi} = \hat{\tilde{\Psi}} - \hat{\Psi}^{\#}\).
psi_tilde_est: The pooled-ATE before bias correction.
psi_pound_est: The estimated bias. If this is near zero, pooling was safe. If it is large, A-TMLE corrected for substantial external data bias.
lower, upper: 95% confidence interval based on the efficient influence curve.
eic: The efficient influence curve values, useful for diagnostics.

title: 28  In development
text:
37.1 Pre-processing: matching for overlap
Before applying either method, ensure that the RCT and RWD populations have adequate covariate overlap. A recommended strategy:

Apply RCT inclusion/exclusion criteria to the RWD to ensure basic comparability.
Estimate the trial enrollment score \(\hat{\Pi}(1 \mid W) = \hat{P}(S = 1 \mid W)\) using the combined data.
Match each RCT patient with \(K\) external patients on the enrollment score (e.g., \(K = 3\) nearest-neighbor matching).
Within the matched sample, estimate the RWD propensity score and optionally apply additional matching.

This two-stage matching makes the trial enrollment score and the RWD propensity score approximately constant across the analysis sample, which improves the finite-sample robustness of both ES-CV-TMLE and A-TMLE.

title: 28  In development
text:
37.2 Diagnostics
After fitting either method, check:

Propensity score overlap: Plot \(\hat{P}(S = 1 \mid W)\); if the RCT and RWD populations have minimal overlap, the external data cannot help and may introduce instability.
Estimated bias magnitude: A-TMLE reports \(\hat{\Psi}^{\#}\) directly. For ES-CV-TMLE, the proportion of folds selecting RCT-only is a proxy for bias severity.
Influence function values: Extreme values suggest near-positivity violations or highly influential observations.

title: 28  In development
text:
37.3 Sensitivity analysis
Even with these methods, the analyst should report:

The RCT-only estimate as a benchmark. If the data-fusion estimate deviates substantially from the RCT-only result, investigate why.
Results under different Super Learner libraries to assess model dependence. For guidance on learner library sensitivity, see Chapter 19.
The proportion of external data retained after matching, and how results change with stricter or looser matching thresholds.

title: 28  In development
text:
38.1 Check your understanding


Q1. Why is naive pooling of RCT and RWD dangerous, even when the RWD sample is much larger?

Because the observational data may contain unmeasured confounding that biases the treatment effect estimate. Naive pooling imports this bias into the combined estimate. The larger RWD sample dominates the pooled analysis, so the bias from the RWD overwhelms the unbiased signal from the small RCT. The resulting confidence interval is narrow (because of the large sample size) but centered on a biased estimate, producing confident wrong answers.



Q2. What is the key difference between the ES-CV-TMLE and A-TMLE strategies?

ES-CV-TMLE makes a binary decision: pool or do not pool, based on a cross-validated bias\(^2\)+variance criterion. A-TMLE takes a continuous approach: it always pools but estimates and subtracts the bias using a flexible working model (HAL). A-TMLE can gain efficiency even when the bias is small but complex (varying across covariate strata), whereas ES-CV-TMLE may fail to detect such bias and either incorrectly pool or conservatively reject.



Q3. Why is the trial enrollment score \(P(S = 1 \mid W)\) important for data fusion?

The trial enrollment score determines the overlap between RCT and RWD populations. If \(P(S = 1 \mid W) \approx 0\) for some covariate strata, those strata have no representation in the RCT, so the treatment effect for those patients cannot be learned from the trial. Borrowing strength from RWD for these strata requires the (untestable) assumption that the treatment effect is the same in the trial and the real world. Making the enrollment score approximately constant through matching reduces dependence on this assumption and improves finite-sample performance.

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.1 Clarifying the Targets: SATE vs PATE vs Site-Specific Effects
When a randomized trial produces an effect estimate, it is natural to ask: “Does this result apply to my patients?” The answer depends on which causal estimand we are targeting.
Sample Average Treatment Effect (SATE): The average treatment effect among individuals enrolled in the trial: \[\text{SATE} = E[Y^{a=1} - Y^{a=0} \mid S = 1]\] where \(S = 1\) indicates trial membership. This is what the trial directly estimates through randomization.
Population Average Treatment Effect (PATE): The average treatment effect in a target population that may differ from the trial sample: \[\text{PATE} = E[Y^{a=1} - Y^{a=0}]\] This is what clinicians and policymakers usually want—the expected effect if the treatment were deployed broadly.
Site-specific or subgroup effects: Treatment effects within particular subpopulations (e.g., a specific hospital, age group, or region). These are relevant when treatment effects are heterogeneous and local decision-making is needed.
The gap between SATE and PATE can be substantial. Trials often enroll younger, healthier, and more adherent patients than the broader population. If the treatment effect varies with these characteristics (effect modification), the SATE may be a poor guide for population-level decisions.
crumbs: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.2 Why Naive Generalization Fails
Three mechanisms cause SATE and PATE to diverge:

29.2.1 Selection Into Trials
Trial participants are not randomly sampled from the target population. Enrollment criteria, willingness to participate, and geographic access all create selection. If the factors driving selection also modify the treatment effect, the trial estimate does not transport.


29.2.2 Effect Modification Across Populations
When the treatment effect varies with baseline covariates \(W\) (e.g., age, comorbidity burden, disease severity), and the distribution of \(W\) differs between trial and target populations, the average effect will differ even if the conditional effects \(E[Y^{a=1} - Y^{a=0} \mid W = w]\) are identical.


29.2.3 Covariate Shift
Even when the conditional treatment effect (given covariates) is the same across populations, differences in the marginal distribution of covariates produce different marginal effects. This is a reweighting problem, and it is the problem that transportability methods solve.






The Transportability Assumption



The key assumption underlying all transportability methods is that conditional on measured covariates, the treatment effect is the same across populations. This is untestable but becomes more plausible as richer covariate sets are available. It is closely related to the “no unmeasured effect modification” assumption.
crumbs: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.3 Assumptions for Transportability
Formally, transporting a causal effect from a trial (\(S = 1\)) to a target population requires three assumptions:

29.3.1 S-Exchangeability (Conditional Independence)
\[Y^a \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid W \quad \text{for } a \in \{0, 1\}\]
Conditional on measured covariates \(W\), the potential outcomes are independent of study membership. In other words, trial participants and target population members with the same covariate profile have the same expected outcomes under each treatment.
This is the transportability assumption. It is violated when unmeasured factors that differ between populations also modify the treatment effect.


29.3.2 S-Positivity
\[P(S = 1 \mid W = w) > 0 \quad \text{for all } w \text{ with } P(W = w) > 0\]
Every covariate profile present in the target population must have some representation in the trial. If the target population includes patient types that were entirely excluded from the trial, transportability is impossible for those patients.


29.3.3 Consistency
\[Y = Y^a \text{ when } A = a\]
The standard consistency assumption: the observed outcome under treatment \(a\) equals the potential outcome under \(a\). This requires that the treatment is implemented the same way in the trial and target population (same drug, dose, protocol).
crumbs: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.4 Methods for Transportability

29.4.1 IOSW: Inverse Odds of Sampling Weights
The simplest approach reweights the trial data to match the target population’s covariate distribution. The inverse odds of sampling weight for individual \(i\) in the trial is:
\[w_i = \frac{P(S = 0 \mid W_i)}{P(S = 1 \mid W_i)} = \frac{1 - P(S = 1 \mid W_i)}{P(S = 1 \mid W_i)}\]
where \(P(S = 1 \mid W)\) is the propensity for study membership, estimated from a combined dataset of trial participants and target population members.
The PATE is then estimated as:
\[\widehat{\text{PATE}} = \frac{\sum_{i: S_i=1, A_i=1} w_i Y_i}{\sum_{i: S_i=1, A_i=1} w_i} - \frac{\sum_{i: S_i=1, A_i=0} w_i Y_i}{\sum_{i: S_i=1, A_i=0} w_i}\]






IOSW Limitations



IOSW depends entirely on correct specification of the study membership model. If this model is wrong, the transported estimate is biased. Additionally, extreme weights (when the trial population is very different from the target) inflate variance and can produce unstable estimates.




29.4.2 Outcome Modeling with Transport
An alternative is to fit an outcome model in the trial data (where randomization ensures unconfounded estimation) and then standardize (g-compute) over the covariate distribution of the target population:
\[\widehat{\text{PATE}} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{target}}} \sum_{i: S_i=0} \left[\hat{E}(Y \mid A=1, W_i) - \hat{E}(Y \mid A=0, W_i)\right]\]
This approach is consistent if the outcome model is correctly specified but does not require correct modeling of study membership.


29.4.3 Doubly Robust Approaches: TMLE for Transportability
A TMLE for transportability combines the IOSW and outcome modeling approaches, providing consistency if either the study membership model or the outcome model is correctly specified.
The procedure:

Estimate the study membership model: \(\hat{P}(S = 1 \mid W)\) using logistic regression or Super Learner
Estimate the outcome model: \(\hat{E}(Y \mid A, W, S = 1)\) using data from the trial
Target the PATE: Apply the TMLE fluctuation step using the efficient influence function for the PATE, which incorporates both the outcome model predictions and the IOSW weights
Compute the transported estimate: Average the targeted predictions over the target population


# Pseudocode for transportability TMLE
# Step 1: Combine trial and target population data
combined <- rbind(trial_data, target_data)
combined$S <- c(rep(1, nrow(trial_data)), rep(0, nrow(target_data)))

# Step 2: Estimate P(S=1 | W) - study membership propensity
ps_model <- SuperLearner(Y = combined$S,
                         X = combined[, covariates],
                         SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.ranger"))
combined$ps_study <- ps_model$SL.predict

# Step 3: Estimate E(Y | A, W) in trial only
outcome_model <- SuperLearner(Y = trial_data$Y,
                              X = trial_data[, c("A", covariates)],
                              SL.library = c("SL.glm", "SL.ranger"))

# Step 4: Predict counterfactuals for target population
target_data$Qbar1 <- predict(outcome_model,
                              newdata = transform(target_data, A = 1))$pred
target_data$Qbar0 <- predict(outcome_model,
                              newdata = transform(target_data, A = 0))$pred

# Step 5: PATE estimate (before targeting step)
PATE_initial <- mean(target_data$Qbar1 - target_data$Qbar0)

# Step 6: Apply TMLE targeting/fluctuation for efficiency and double robustness
# (Full implementation requires the efficient influence function for the PATE)



29.4.4 Connection to RCT-RWD Hybrid Designs
The transportability framework connects directly to the hybrid designs discussed in Chapter 28. In that chapter, external real-world data is used to augment trial evidence. Transportability methods formalize when and how this augmentation is valid:

External controls: Target population outcome data under control is available from RWD; the trial provides the treatment arm. IOSW reweights trial participants to match the RWD population.
RCT as anchor: The trial provides internally valid estimates; RWD provides the target population covariate distribution for generalization.

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.5 Diagnostics for Covariate Shift
Before transporting trial results, you must assess how different the trial and target populations are.

29.5.1 Propensity for Study Membership
Fit a model for \(P(S = 1 \mid W)\) and examine the distribution:

set.seed(2026)

# Simulate trial and target populations
n_trial <- 300
n_target <- 1000

# Trial enrolls younger, healthier patients
trial_age <- rnorm(n_trial, mean = 55, sd = 8)
trial_comorbidity <- rbinom(n_trial, 1, 0.15)
trial_severity <- rnorm(n_trial, mean = 2, sd = 0.8)

# Target population is older, sicker
target_age <- rnorm(n_target, mean = 65, sd = 12)
target_comorbidity <- rbinom(n_target, 1, 0.40)
target_severity <- rnorm(n_target, mean = 3.5, sd = 1.2)

# Combine
combined <- data.frame(
  age = c(trial_age, target_age),
  comorbidity = c(trial_comorbidity, target_comorbidity),
  severity = c(trial_severity, target_severity),
  S = c(rep(1, n_trial), rep(0, n_target))
)

# Fit study membership model
ps_model <- glm(S ~ age + comorbidity + severity,
                data = combined, family = binomial)
combined$ps <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

# Plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Propensity score distribution
hist(combined$ps[combined$S == 1], breaks = 30, col = rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5),
     main = "P(S=1 | W)", xlab = "Propensity for trial membership",
     xlim = c(0, 1), freq = FALSE)
hist(combined$ps[combined$S == 0], breaks = 30, col = rgb(0.8, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3),
     add = TRUE, freq = FALSE)
legend("topright", c("Trial (S=1)", "Target (S=0)"),
       fill = c(rgb(0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5), rgb(0.8, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3)))

# IOSW weights
trial_idx <- combined$S == 1
iosw <- (1 - combined$ps[trial_idx]) / combined$ps[trial_idx]
iosw_stabilized <- iosw / mean(iosw)

hist(iosw_stabilized, breaks = 30, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Stabilized IOSW weights", xlab = "Weight")
abline(v = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat(sprintf("Effective sample size: %.0f / %d (%.0f%%)\n",
            sum(iosw_stabilized)^2 / sum(iosw_stabilized^2),
            n_trial,
            100 * (sum(iosw_stabilized)^2 / sum(iosw_stabilized^2)) / n_trial))

Effective sample size: 41 / 300 (14%)








Figure 29.1: Propensity for study membership: overlap between trial and target population







29.5.2 Standardized Mean Differences
Compare covariate distributions before and after reweighting:

# Compute standardized mean differences
compute_smd <- function(x_trial, x_target, weights = NULL) {
  if (is.null(weights)) {
    mean_diff <- mean(x_trial) - mean(x_target)
  } else {
    mean_diff <- weighted.mean(x_trial, weights) - mean(x_target)
  }
  pooled_sd <- sqrt((var(x_trial) + var(x_target)) / 2)
  return(mean_diff / pooled_sd)
}

covars <- c("age", "comorbidity", "severity")
smd_before <- sapply(covars, function(v)
  compute_smd(combined[[v]][trial_idx], combined[[v]][!trial_idx]))
smd_after <- sapply(covars, function(v)
  compute_smd(combined[[v]][trial_idx], combined[[v]][!trial_idx],
              weights = iosw_stabilized))

smd_df <- data.frame(
  covariate = rep(covars, 2),
  smd = c(smd_before, smd_after),
  status = rep(c("Before IOSW", "After IOSW"), each = length(covars))
)

# Dot plot
plot(1:length(covars), abs(smd_before), pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 1.5,
     xlim = c(0.5, length(covars) + 0.5), ylim = c(0, max(abs(smd_before)) * 1.1),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Absolute SMD", main = "Covariate Balance: Trial vs Target",
     xaxt = "n")
points(1:length(covars), abs(smd_after), pch = 17, col = "blue", cex = 1.5)
axis(1, at = 1:length(covars), labels = covars)
abline(h = 0.1, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
text(length(covars), 0.12, "SMD = 0.1 threshold", col = "gray50", cex = 0.8, adj = 1)
legend("topright", c("Before IOSW", "After IOSW"),
       pch = c(19, 17), col = c("red", "blue"))







Figure 29.2: Standardized mean differences before and after IOSW reweighting

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
section: 29.6 Worked Example: SATE vs PATE Divergence
text:
29.6 Worked Example: SATE vs PATE Divergence
We demonstrate how effect modification produces divergence between the trial-specific effect and the population effect.

set.seed(2026)

# --- Data generation with effect modification ---
n_trial <- 300
n_target <- 1000

# Trial population (younger)
W_trial <- rnorm(n_trial, mean = 55, sd = 8)
A_trial <- rbinom(n_trial, 1, 0.5)  # randomized

# Target population (older)
W_target <- rnorm(n_target, mean = 65, sd = 12)

# Treatment effect INCREASES with age (effect modification)
# Y = 10 + 0.1*age + A * (0.5 + 0.05 * (age - 50)) + noise
# At age 55: effect = 0.5 + 0.05*5 = 0.75
# At age 65: effect = 0.5 + 0.05*15 = 1.25
tau <- function(age) 0.5 + 0.05 * (age - 50)

Y_trial <- 10 + 0.1 * W_trial + A_trial * tau(W_trial) + rnorm(n_trial, 0, 1)

# SATE: treatment effect estimated in trial
sate_est <- mean(Y_trial[A_trial == 1]) - mean(Y_trial[A_trial == 0])

# True SATE (analytical)
true_sate <- mean(tau(W_trial))

# True PATE (analytical)
true_pate <- mean(tau(W_target))

# IOSW-transported estimate
combined_w <- c(W_trial, W_target)
combined_s <- c(rep(1, n_trial), rep(0, n_target))
ps_fit <- glm(combined_s ~ combined_w, family = binomial)
ps_hat <- predict(ps_fit, type = "response")
ps_trial <- ps_hat[1:n_trial]
iosw <- (1 - ps_trial) / ps_trial
iosw_stab <- iosw / mean(iosw)

pate_iosw <- weighted.mean(Y_trial[A_trial == 1], iosw_stab[A_trial == 1]) -
             weighted.mean(Y_trial[A_trial == 0], iosw_stab[A_trial == 0])

cat("=== SATE vs PATE with Effect Modification ===\n")

=== SATE vs PATE with Effect Modification ===

cat(sprintf("True SATE (trial population):   %.3f\n", true_sate))

True SATE (trial population):   0.767

cat(sprintf("Estimated SATE (naive):         %.3f\n", sate_est))

Estimated SATE (naive):         0.983

cat(sprintf("True PATE (target population):  %.3f\n", true_pate))

True PATE (target population):  1.245

cat(sprintf("Estimated PATE (IOSW):          %.3f\n", pate_iosw))

Estimated PATE (IOSW):          1.097

cat(sprintf("\nDivergence (PATE - SATE):       %.3f\n", true_pate - true_sate))


Divergence (PATE - SATE):       0.478

cat("\nThe target population is older, and the treatment effect\n")


The target population is older, and the treatment effect

cat("increases with age, so PATE > SATE.\n")

increases with age, so PATE > SATE.


In this example, the treatment effect increases with age. Because the target population is older than the trial population, the PATE exceeds the SATE. A clinician treating the target population who relied on the trial’s SATE would underestimate the treatment benefit. The IOSW-transported estimate corrects for this by upweighting older trial participants.

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.7 Connection to ES-CV-TMLE and A-TMLE
The transportability framework connects to the adaptive methods discussed in the context of RCT-RWD hybrid designs. Specifically:

ES-CV-TMLE (Experiment-Selector Cross-Validated TMLE) uses cross-validation to select the optimal combination of trial and external data for estimating the PATE, automatically downweighting external data that introduces bias.
A-TMLE (Adaptive TMLE) adapts to the degree of similarity between trial and external populations, achieving efficiency gains when populations are similar while protecting against bias when they are not.

Both methods can be viewed as adaptive transportability estimators: they solve the transportability problem while being robust to violations of the transportability assumption. See Chapter 28 for details.
crumbs: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis

title: 29  Transportability and Generalizability in RCT-RWD Synthesis
text:
29.8 Check Your Understanding






Questions




SATE vs PATE: A trial of a blood pressure medication enrolls patients aged 40-65 with no diabetes. The effect estimate is a 5 mmHg reduction. The target population includes patients aged 40-85, 30% of whom have diabetes. Under what conditions does the trial SATE equal the PATE? Under what conditions might they diverge?
S-positivity: You are transporting results from a trial that excluded patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min. Your target population includes such patients (15% of the population). Can you estimate the PATE using transportability methods? What could you do instead?
Diagnostics: After computing IOSW weights to transport a trial result to your target population, you find that the effective sample size is 18 (from a trial of 400 patients). What does this mean, and what are your options?









Answers






SATE equals PATE if there is no effect modification by age or diabetes status—that is, if the treatment works equally well regardless of age and diabetes. They will diverge if older patients or patients with diabetes respond differently to the medication. For example, if the drug is less effective in patients with impaired kidney function (which correlates with both age and diabetes), the PATE could be attenuated relative to the SATE.
S-positivity is violated: the trial has zero probability of enrolling patients with eGFR < 30, so there are no trial data to reweight for this subgroup. You cannot estimate the PATE for the full target population. Options: (a) Restrict the PATE to the subpopulation with eGFR >= 30 and report this limitation. (b) Use external data (RWD) for the eGFR < 30 subgroup, but this requires strong assumptions about the treatment effect in this group. (c) Conduct a sensitivity analysis exploring plausible treatment effects in the excluded subgroup.
An ESS of 18 from 400 trial participants means extreme covariate shift: the trial population is very different from the target, and a few trial participants are receiving enormous weights. This makes the transported estimate highly variable and unreliable. Options: (a) Examine which covariates drive the divergence and consider whether all are necessary for transportability. (b) Trim extreme weights and report as a sensitivity analysis. (c) Collect additional trial data from centers that are more representative of the target population. (d) Use a doubly robust method (TMLE) which may be more stable than pure IOSW.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.1 1. The assumption you cannot test, and usually cannot trust
Instrumental variables, negative controls, and proximal inference when adjustment is not enough
Estimated reading time: 35 minutes
Every method in this handbook so far rests on the same load-bearing assumption: that the measured covariates are enough to remove confounding, so that treated and untreated patients with the same covariate values are comparable. The Causal Roadmap (Chapter 5) calls it conditional exchangeability, and it is the one assumption the data cannot check. In pharmacoepidemiology it is also the assumption most likely to fail. Sicker patients are treated more aggressively, healthier patients adhere better, and the frailty or disease severity that drives both treatment and outcome is rarely captured fully in claims or records. When adjustment is not credible no matter how rich the covariate set, three strategies let an analysis make progress by trading the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption for a different structural assumption that may be easier to defend in the problem at hand.
Confounding by indication is the standard cautionary example. A drug prescribed to the sickest patients will look harmful in a crude comparison, and look harmful still after adjusting for the severity markers that happen to be recorded, because the part of severity that drove the prescribing decision is never fully measured. The healthy-user effect runs the other way: patients who start a preventive therapy tend to be more health-conscious in ways that also lower their risk, so the therapy looks protective beyond its true effect. In both cases adding more covariates helps only to the extent that the new covariates capture the unmeasured driver, and the analyst has no way to know from the data when enough has been captured.
The strategies below share a common move. Each introduces an extra variable, an instrument or a negative control or a proxy, whose relationship to treatment and outcome is constrained by subject-matter knowledge rather than by the data. That constraint replaces the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption with a new one. The new assumption is still untestable, but it is a different kind of claim, and in the right problem it is far more defensible because it follows from a known mechanism.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.2 2. Instrumental variables
Sometimes the data contain a hidden coin flip. Which physician a patient happened to see, not how sick they were, tipped the treatment one way or the other, and that accident is what lets us learn the effect. An instrument is a variable that nudges treatment without otherwise touching the outcome. Formally it must satisfy three conditions: it is associated with treatment (relevance); it affects the outcome only through treatment (the exclusion restriction); and it shares no common cause with the outcome (independence). A classic pharmacoepidemiologic instrument is a physician’s or facility’s prescribing preference. Two patients who happen to see a doctor with a strong preference for drug A versus drug B are, on average, exchangeable in their own characteristics, yet they receive different treatments because of the prescriber, so the prescriber’s preference nudges treatment without being caused by the patient’s prognosis. Calendar-time policy changes and, in genetic epidemiology, an inherited variant used in Mendelian randomization, play the same role.
What an instrument buys is identification without measuring the confounder, because the instrument induces variation in treatment that is unrelated to the unmeasured driver. What it costs is twofold and worth stating plainly. First, the estimand changes. Under a monotonicity assumption, an instrument identifies the effect among the patients whose treatment the instrument actually moved, the so-called compliers, not the average effect in the whole population. In the prescribing-preference example, that is the effect among patients whose treatment would differ depending on which physician they happened to see, which is a real and policy-relevant group but not the same as everyone. Second, the exclusion restriction and independence are themselves untestable, and a weak instrument, one only loosely associated with treatment, produces estimates that are both imprecise and biased toward the confounded answer. A credible instrumental-variable analysis therefore leans on a strong, mechanistically justified instrument and reports the local nature of the effect it identifies.
The targeted-learning toolkit extends to instrumental-variable estimands: doubly robust and machine-learning-based estimators of the local effect exist and use the same Super Learner nuisance machinery seen elsewhere in this book. The example below contrasts a naive confounded estimate with a two-stage least-squares instrumental-variable estimate on simulated data.


Show code
set.seed(2026)
n  <- 4000
U  <- rnorm(n)                                   # unmeasured confounder (severity)
Z  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                          # instrument: prescriber preference
A  <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.2 + 1.3 * Z + 0.9 * U))   # treatment depends on Z and U
Y  <- 0.5 + 0.0 * A + 1.0 * U + rnorm(n)         # TRUE treatment effect is 0; U confounds

# Naive: regress outcome on treatment, ignoring U (biased by confounding)
naive <- coef(lm(Y ~ A))["A"]

# Instrumental-variable (two-stage least squares) estimate of the effect
fs   <- lm(A ~ Z)                                # stage 1: treatment on instrument
Ahat <- predict(fs)
iv   <- coef(lm(Y ~ Ahat))["Ahat"]               # stage 2: outcome on predicted treatment

c(naive = round(naive, 3), iv = round(iv, 3))    # naive far from 0; IV near 0


naive.A iv.Ahat 
  0.655  -0.039 


The naive coefficient picks up the confounding through U and points to an effect that is not there, while the instrumental-variable estimate, using only the variation in treatment that the instrument induced, recovers the true null. That is the whole appeal of the design, achieved without ever measuring U.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.3 3. Negative controls
A negative control is a variable chosen so that one of its causal links is known to be absent, which lets it act as a tripwire for confounding. A negative control outcome is an outcome the treatment cannot plausibly cause, yet which shares the confounding structure of the real outcome. A negative control exposure is an exposure that cannot plausibly cause the real outcome, yet which shares the same confounders. If a careful analysis finds a treatment effect on a negative control outcome, or an effect of the negative control exposure on the real outcome, the most likely explanation is residual confounding, because the causal link that would explain it is known to be absent.
The canonical example comes from influenza-vaccine studies. Vaccinated older adults appeared to have much lower all-cause mortality than unvaccinated peers, including before the influenza season had begun. Death in the pre-season period is a negative control outcome: the vaccine cannot prevent deaths from influenza that has not yet circulated, so the apparent benefit in that window had to be confounding, the healthy-vaccinee effect, and it called the headline estimate into question. The NSAID-and-fracture check in Chapter 19 is the same idea applied as a diagnostic.
Used this way a negative control is a falsification test: it can reveal bias but does not by itself remove it. The value of a clean negative control is real, because an analysis that passes a well-chosen falsification test is more credible than one that was never challenged. The next strategy turns the negative control from a test into an estimator.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.4 4. Proximal causal inference
Proximal causal inference starts from a simple observation. If a negative control carries information about the unmeasured confounder, then with enough negative controls of the right kinds it should be possible not just to detect the bias but to remove it. The setup uses two proxies of the unmeasured confounder: one connected to the treatment side, sometimes called a treatment-inducing proxy, and one connected to the outcome side, which is essentially a negative control outcome. Neither proxy measures the confounder directly, and neither alone is enough. Used together, under conditions that link them to the hidden confounder, they identify the causal effect through a pair of equations, called bridge functions, that play the role the unmeasured confounder would have played if it had been observed.
The intuition is worth holding onto even without the equations. Two imperfect, noisy measurements of the same hidden variable can, in combination, stand in for that variable in a way that neither could alone, much as two angles fix a position that one angle leaves ambiguous. A concrete pharmacoepidemiologic instance: baseline disease severity is unmeasured, but a pre-treatment lab value related to how aggressively a clinician treats serves as the treatment-side proxy, while a pre-treatment symptom score related to prognosis serves as the outcome-side proxy. Proximal methods combine the two to recover the effect that adjustment alone could not.
Proximal inference is the most technically demanding of the three strategies and is an active research area. It requires genuinely valid proxies and additional completeness conditions that are themselves untestable, and the estimators, including targeted-learning versions, are still maturing in available software. The practical posture for now is to understand it as the principled destination that negative controls point toward, to collect candidate proxies prospectively when a study is being designed, and to consult the current methodological literature before attempting an applied proximal analysis.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
section: 30.5 5. Choosing a strategy, and how each one fails
text:
30.5 5. Choosing a strategy, and how each one fails
These three strategies do not compete so much as suit different situations, and each fails in a characteristic way. An instrumental-variable analysis lives or dies on the instrument: a strong, mechanistically justified instrument such as a genuine prescribing preference can be compelling, while a weak or arguable one delivers an estimate that is imprecise and quietly biased back toward the confounded answer, and even a perfect instrument identifies only the effect among the patients it moved. A negative-control analysis depends on finding a control that truly shares the confounding structure while being genuinely unaffected by the causal link in question; a poorly chosen control either misses real bias or raises a false alarm. Proximal inference depends on two valid proxies and conditions that are hard to verify, and on software and expertise that are still developing.
The common thread is that none of these strategies escapes untestable assumptions; they relocate them. The reason to reach for one is that its assumption follows from something you know about how the data were generated, a known prescribing mechanism, a biologically impossible link, a measured proxy for a known confounder, rather than from the hope that the covariate list is complete. When that substantive justification is absent, the honest move is a sensitivity analysis (Chapter 19) that reports how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the result, not a switch to a design whose own assumptions are no more defensible.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.6 Connections to other chapters
This chapter addresses the identification step of the Causal Roadmap (Chapter 5) for the case where its central assumption is not credible. Negative controls appear in Chapter 19 as a falsification diagnostic; here they are framed as the entry point to an estimation strategy. Transportability (Chapter 29) tackles a different identification problem, generalizing an effect to a new population rather than removing unmeasured confounding within one.

title: 30  Identification Beyond Conditional Exchangeability
text:
30.8 Check your understanding


Q1. Why does an instrumental-variable analysis usually estimate something other than the average treatment effect?

Under the standard monotonicity assumption, an instrument identifies the effect only among the patients whose treatment the instrument actually changed, the compliers. Patients who would take the same treatment regardless of the instrument contribute no information about the effect, so the estimate is local to the moved subgroup. This complier effect is real and often policy-relevant, but it is not the population average effect and should be reported as what it is.



Q2. A reviewer asks you to add a negative control outcome to a study of a drug and stroke. What makes a good choice, and what does a non-null result mean?

A good negative control outcome is something the drug cannot plausibly cause within the study window but that is subject to the same confounding as stroke, for example an outcome driven by the same frailty and healthcare-seeking behavior. If the analysis estimates a non-null effect on that control, the causal link that would explain it is known to be absent, so the finding points to residual confounding biasing the main estimate. It detects the problem; it does not by itself fix it.



Q3. In one sentence, how does proximal causal inference go beyond a negative control?

A negative control uses one proxy of the unmeasured confounder to test for bias, whereas proximal inference combines a treatment-side proxy and an outcome-side proxy to actually identify and remove the effect of the unmeasured confounder, turning the diagnostic into an estimator.

title: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study
text:
31.1 What a naive analysis might have done
Estimated reading time: 10 minutes
Throughout this handbook, we have used the longitudinal HIV antiretroviral therapy cohort to illustrate every major concept, from defining causal questions to diagnosing estimator behavior (Petersen and Laan 2014; Hernán and Robins 2025). See the Running Case Study for the full data description, including the variable dictionary and target trial protocol. This final section draws the lessons together and traces the progression from naive methods to principled causal estimation. See the Running Case Study for the data description and variable dictionary.
Without the roadmap, a researcher would likely fit a Cox or pooled logistic regression, adjust for time-varying CD4 because it is a confounder, and report the hazard ratio as the effect of HAART. Two of those moves are the traps developed earlier in the book. Adjusting for CD4 blocks part of the treatment effect, because CD4 is also affected by prior treatment (Chapter 14), and the hazard ratio answers a different question from the one a clinician asks (Chapter 4). As the running case study shows, the result can make an effective treatment look harmful.
crumbs: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study

title: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study
section: 31.2 How the Causal Roadmap clarified the question
text:
31.2 How the Causal Roadmap clarified the question
Running the seven steps of Chapter 5 on this cohort fixed each of those problems before any model was fit. A target trial protocol set the question (the effect on mortality of initiating HAART at seroconversion versus not); a DAG made the dual role of CD4, a confounder of future treatment and a mediator of past treatment, explicit; the estimand was the marginal risk difference rather than a hazard ratio; and the identification assumptions (exchangeability, consistency, positivity) were stated together with where they might fail, namely unmeasured adherence and clinical staging. Only then were g-computation, IPTW, and TMLE applied and compared.
crumbs: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study

title: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study
section: 31.3 Why time-dependent confounding required longitudinal methods
text:
31.3 Why time-dependent confounding required longitudinal methods
The central lesson of this case study is that standard regression cannot handle treatment-confounder feedback. When a time-varying confounder (cd4.sqrt) is both a consequence of prior treatment (haartind) and a cause of future treatment, the analyst faces an impossible choice in a regression framework:

Do not adjust for time-varying CD4: leaves confounding of future treatment unaddressed.
Adjust for time-varying CD4: blocks part of the treatment effect and introduces collider bias.

Neither option produces a consistent estimate of the causal effect, as demonstrated concretely in Chapter 14. The g-methods (g-computation, IPTW with marginal structural models, longitudinal TMLE) resolve this dilemma by modeling the treatment mechanism separately from the outcome and using that model to reweight or standardize the analysis. Chapter 14 walked through the mechanics of longitudinal TMLE step by step, showing how backwards sequential regression conditions on cd4.sqrt where it confounds future treatment and integrates it out where it mediates past treatment. This is not a minor technical improvement; it is a qualitative change in what can be estimated.
crumbs: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study

title: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study
section: 31.4 What the example illustrates about real-world evidence analyses
text:
31.4 What the example illustrates about real-world evidence analyses
The HIV/HAART example is not unique. Treatment-confounder feedback arises whenever:

Treatment decisions respond to time-varying patient status (lab values, symptoms, disease progression)
Those same patient characteristics are also affected by prior treatment
The outcome of interest occurs at the end of a follow-up period during which both treatment and confounders evolve

This pattern is ubiquitous in chronic disease epidemiology, pharmacoepidemiology, and comparative effectiveness research. Examples include:

Insulin dose adjustments based on HbA1c in diabetes
Immunosuppressant dosing based on kidney function in transplant recipients
Chemotherapy regimen changes based on tumor markers in oncology
Blood pressure medication titration based on BP readings

In all of these settings, the methods covered in this handbook, not standard regression, are needed to estimate causal effects correctly. The Causal Roadmap provides the structure, and the estimation methods (g-computation, IPTW, TMLE, longitudinal TMLE) provide the tools.
crumbs: 31  Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study

  ~Approach, ~`Handles confounding`, ~`Handles feedback`, ~`Marginal effect`, ~`Valid inference`,

Even after applying longitudinal methods, the results depend on untestable identification assumptions. Chapter 19 showed how to probe this dependence using E-values, quantitative bias analysis, and truncation sensitivity. For the HAART cohort, unmeasured adherence is the most plausible threat: patients who adhere to treatment tend to be healthier, potentially inflating the apparent benefit. Sensitivity analysis quantifies how strong this confounding would need to be to explain away the estimated effect.
The progression from naive regression to longitudinal TMLE is not just methodological sophistication for its own sake. Each step solves a real problem that the previous approach could not handle. The antiretroviral therapy case study makes those problems, and their solutions, concrete.

title: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms
text:
32.1 Causal framework and study design
This glossary collects abbreviations and short technical terms used throughout the handbook. Each entry gives a one- to two-sentence definition and, where useful, a pointer to the chapter that develops the concept in depth. It is intended as a quick reference, not as a substitute for the worked examples in the chapters themselves.
ATE: Average Treatment Effect. The expected difference in potential outcomes if everyone in the target population were treated vs. if no one were treated: \(E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\). The default estimand for most chapters in this handbook. See Chapter 4.
ATT: Average Treatment Effect on the Treated. The expected difference in potential outcomes restricted to people who actually received treatment: \(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid A = 1]\).
Causal estimand. A summary of potential outcomes (e.g., the ATE) defined before any statistical procedure is chosen. Contrasted with a statistical estimand, which is a function of the observed-data distribution that equals the causal estimand under the identification assumptions. See Chapter 5, Step 3.
Causal gap. The difference between a causal estimand and the statistical estimand a procedure actually targets, which is nonzero whenever an identification assumption fails. Cannot be estimated directly; can be bounded by sensitivity analysis.
Causal Roadmap. The seven-step framework (question, structural causal model, estimand, identification, estimation, sensitivity analysis, interpretation) used to organize every analysis in this handbook. See Chapter 5.
Clean-room workflow. An analysis protocol in which the full statistical analysis plan (including estimator, nuisance learners, diagnostics, and stopping rules) is locked before the outcome data are seen, often with formal staging and external review. Reduces the credibility cost of investigator degrees of freedom in observational analyses.
DAG: Directed Acyclic Graph. A graph in which nodes are variables and directed arrows encode assumed causal relationships, with no directed cycles. Used to encode the structural causal model and to read off identification conditions. See Chapter 5, Step 2.
Estimand. The quantity we are trying to estimate, defined independently of the estimator used. See causal estimand and statistical estimand.
HTE: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects. Settings in which the treatment effect varies across subgroups defined by covariates; the object of estimation is usually the CATE.
ICH E9(R1). International Council for Harmonisation guideline on statistical principles for clinical trials, addendum on estimands and sensitivity analyses. Provides the regulatory framework for defining intercurrent-event strategies and aligning estimands with the scientific question. See Chapter 25.
ITT: Intention-to-Treat. Analysis strategy that classifies participants according to their assigned (or, in observational analogues, baseline) treatment, regardless of subsequent adherence or switching.
OR / RR / RD: Odds Ratio / Risk Ratio / Risk Difference. Three common scales for binary-outcome contrasts. The RD is the default in this handbook because it is collapsible and directly interpretable as an absolute risk change.
PP: Per-Protocol. Analysis strategy that estimates the effect of adhering to a treatment strategy, in contrast to ITT.
RCT: Randomized Controlled Trial. A study in which treatment is assigned by randomization, so baseline exchangeability holds by design.
RWD / RWE: Real-World Data / Real-World Evidence. Data collected outside controlled clinical trials (RWD) and the evidence derived from analyzing such data (RWE). The handbook treats RWE as observational target-trial emulation.
SCM: Structural Causal Model. A non-parametric system of structural equations representing the data-generating process. The DAG is a graphical projection of the SCM. See Chapter 5, Step 2.
SWIG: Single-World Intervention Graph. A graph that combines factual and counterfactual variables on a single diagram to read off identification under interventions. Used in some chapters but not the default presentation.
Target trial. A hypothetical randomized trial that the observational analysis is designed to emulate. The target trial protocol forces the analyst to specify eligibility, time zero, treatment strategies, assignment, outcome, follow-up, contrast, and analysis plan up front. See Chapter 5, Step 1.
Time zero / \(t_0\). The moment at which eligibility, treatment assignment, and the start of follow-up coincide in the target trial. Misalignment of time zero is the source of immortal-time bias.
crumbs: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms

title: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms
text:
32.2 Identification assumptions
Consistency. The potential outcome under treatment value \(a\) equals the observed outcome for individuals who actually received \(a\): \(Y(a) = Y\) when \(A = a\).
Exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding). Conditional on measured covariates \(W\), the potential outcomes are independent of the treatment assignment: \(Y(a) \perp A \mid W\).
Sequential exchangeability. The longitudinal extension of exchangeability: at each time point, the future potential outcomes are independent of the current treatment given covariate and treatment history.
Positivity / overlap. Every covariate stratum has nonzero probability of receiving each treatment value: \(0 < P(A = a \mid W) < 1\). Practical positivity violations occur when this probability is technically nonzero but extreme; structural violations occur when it is exactly zero by design or definition. See Chapter 12.
crumbs: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms

title: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms
text:
32.3 Estimation
AIPW: Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting. A doubly robust estimator that combines an outcome regression with an inverse-probability-of-treatment weighted residual term. Consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified. See Chapter 8.
CATE: Conditional Average Treatment Effect. The treatment effect for individuals with a specified covariate profile: \(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid W = w]\). The object of estimation in the heterogeneity chapters. See Chapter 21.
DGP: Data-Generating Process. The (typically unknown) probabilistic mechanism that produced the observed data, often denoted \(P_0\). Simulation-based work defines the DGP explicitly; observational work treats it as an unknown to be estimated under structural assumptions.
G-computation. Estimation by fitting an outcome model, predicting each unit’s outcome under each treatment value, and averaging across the sample. The point-treatment instance of the g-formula. See Chapter 6.
G-formula / g-methods. The collection of identification formulas and estimation strategies (g-computation, IPTW with MSMs, g-estimation of structural nested models, TMLE) that handle time-varying treatments and confounders in the presence of treatment–confounder feedback.
HAL: Highly Adaptive Lasso. A non-parametric estimator with a convergence-rate guarantee fast enough to support efficient TMLE without sample-splitting. Used as a Super Learner candidate or as the nuisance estimator directly.
IOSW: Inverse Odds of Sampling Weights. Weights used in transportability and generalizability analyses to reweight a study sample so that it represents a target population. See Chapter 29.
IPCW: Inverse Probability of Censoring Weighting. Weights used to adjust for dependent (informative) censoring in time-to-event and longitudinal analyses.
IPTW: Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting. Estimation by reweighting each individual by the inverse of their estimated probability of having received the treatment they actually got, so that the weighted sample mimics one in which treatment was randomized. See Chapter 7.
L-TMLE: Longitudinal TMLE. Extension of TMLE to longitudinal settings with multiple time points, time-varying treatments, and time-varying confounders. Implemented in the ltmle package. See Chapter 14.
LMTP: Longitudinal Modified Treatment Policies. A framework (and R package) for evaluating shift-style and dynamic-regime interventions in longitudinal data, particularly useful when static “always-treat” interventions violate positivity. See Chapter 2 and Part V.
MSM: Marginal Structural Model. A model for the marginal distribution of potential outcomes as a function of treatment strategy, typically fitted by IPTW. The original g-method for time-varying treatments.
Nuisance function. A component of the target parameter that is not itself of scientific interest but must be estimated en route, for example the propensity score and outcome regression in AIPW/TMLE.
Propensity score. \(P(A = 1 \mid W)\), the probability of treatment given covariates. The basis of IPTW and a key diagnostic for overlap.
SL: Super Learner. A cross-validated ensemble of candidate algorithms that selects the convex combination minimizing cross-validated risk. The default nuisance estimator throughout this handbook. See Chapter 9.
TMLE: Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation. A doubly robust, semiparametric efficient estimator that updates an initial outcome estimate using a targeting step driven by the propensity score, yielding asymptotically normal estimates and valid confidence intervals under weak conditions on the nuisance estimators. See Chapter 8.
crumbs: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms

title: 32  Glossary of Abbreviations and Terms
text:
32.4 Clinical / pharmacoepidemiology
ART / HAART. Antiretroviral therapy / Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy. The combination antiretroviral regimens used in the running HIV case study; HAART is the historical term from the cohort era and is used throughout because the literature this dataset comes from uses it.
CD4. CD4+ T-cell count (cells/µL), the principal time-varying confounder in the HIV case study. Low CD4 is both a marker of disease severity (and therefore mortality risk) and a clinical trigger for initiating HAART.
Confounding by indication. The bias arising when the underlying disease severity that prompts treatment is also prognostic for the outcome, so that crude treated-vs-untreated comparisons reflect prognosis rather than the treatment effect.
Immortal time bias. The bias that arises when person-time before a treatment-defining event is misclassified as “exposed,” guaranteeing survival for the early portion of follow-up. Caught by correctly aligning time zero with treatment assignment. See Chapter 5.
Treatment–confounder feedback. The longitudinal pattern in which a time-varying covariate (e.g., CD4) is simultaneously a confounder of future treatment and a consequence of past treatment, so that no single regression can adjust for it without introducing bias. Motivates g-methods. See Chapter 14.
