title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
text:
34 Notation Cheat-Sheet
A one-page reference for the symbols used throughout the handbook. Each chapter defines terms at first use; this page collects them so a reader can look one up without backtracking. The running example is the HIV antiretroviral therapy cohort, so the plain-language column uses it where helpful.

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
text:
34.1 Observed data








Symbol
Name
Plain meaning




\(W\)
Baseline covariates
What we know before treatment: age, sex, baseline CD4. The confounders we adjust for.


\(A\)
Treatment or exposure
Usually binary: \(A=1\) initiated HAART, \(A=0\) did not.


\(Y\)
Outcome
The event of interest, for example death within follow-up.


\(O\)
One observation
The full record for a patient, \(O=(W,A,Y)\) in the point-treatment case.


\(C\)
Censoring indicator
Marks a patient lost to follow-up before the outcome is observed.


\(T\)
Event time
Time to the outcome in survival settings.


\(n\)
Sample size
Number of patients (or person-visits) in the analysis.

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
text:
34.2 Longitudinal and special-setting symbols








Symbol
Name
Plain meaning




\(L_t\)
Time-varying covariate at visit \(t\)
For example CD4 measured at each visit; both confounder and consequence of past treatment.


\(A_t\)
Treatment at visit \(t\)
Treatment decision at visit \(t\).


\(\bar A_t = (A_1,\dots,A_t)\)
Treatment history
All treatment decisions up to visit \(t\).


\(\bar a\)
A treatment regime
A full sequence of assigned treatments, for example “always treat” \(=(1,\dots,1)\).


\(d(W)\)
Treatment rule
A decision: given covariates \(W\), what treatment to assign (Chapter 23).


\(M\)
Mediator
A variable on the pathway from treatment to outcome (Chapter 24).


\(Z\)
Instrument
Affects treatment but not the outcome except through treatment (Chapter 30).


\(S\)
Study/sample indicator
Marks trial versus target population in transportability (Chapter 29).

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
text:
34.3 Potential outcomes and causal estimands








Symbol
Name
Plain meaning




\(Y^a\) or \(Y(a)\)
Potential outcome
The outcome a patient would have had under treatment value \(a\), possibly contrary to fact.


\(E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\)
Average treatment effect (ATE)
Average outcome difference if everyone were treated versus if no one were.


\(\tau(W)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid W]\)
Conditional average treatment effect (CATE)
The ATE within a covariate profile: who benefits more (Chapter 21).


Risk difference / risk ratio / odds ratio
Effect scales
Absolute, relative, and odds contrasts of the two potential-outcome risks. The risk difference is the handbook default.


RMST
Restricted mean survival time
Average event-free time up to a horizon; a survival estimand (Chapter 25).


\(V(d)=E[Y^{d(W)}]\)
Value of a rule
Average outcome if everyone followed rule \(d\) (Chapter 23).

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
section: 34.4 Nuisance functions and the targeted-learning machinery
text:
34.4 Nuisance functions and the targeted-learning machinery








Symbol
Name
Plain meaning




\(Q(A,W)=E[Y\mid A,W]\)
Outcome regression
The model predicting the outcome from treatment and covariates. Also written \(\bar Q\).


\(g(W)=P(A=1\mid W)\)
Propensity score
The model predicting treatment from covariates.


\(Q^*\)
Targeted outcome model
The outcome model after TMLE’s update (fluctuation) step.


\(H\)
Clever covariate
The term that carries propensity information into the TMLE update (Chapter 8).


\(\epsilon\)
Fluctuation parameter
The size of the TMLE update; near zero when the initial fit already balanced treatment.


\(\Psi\), \(\hat\Psi\)
Estimand mapping, estimate
\(\Psi\) turns a data distribution into the target number; \(\hat\Psi\) is its sample estimate.


\(D(O)\)
Efficient influence function
How much one patient pulls the estimate; its spread gives the standard error (Chapter 8).


\(P_0\), \(P_n\)
True and empirical distributions
The unknown data-generating distribution, and the observed sample standing in for it.

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
text:
34.5 Identification assumptions








Assumption
Statement
Plain meaning




Consistency
\(Y = Y(a)\) when \(A=a\)
The observed outcome equals the potential outcome for the treatment actually received; the intervention is well defined.


Exchangeability
\(Y(a) \perp A \mid W\)
No unmeasured confounding: within covariate strata, treatment is as good as randomized.


Positivity
\(0 < g(W) < 1\)
Every covariate profile has some chance of each treatment, so a comparison is possible (Chapter 12).

title: 33  Notation Cheat-Sheet
section: 34.6 Estimators and tools, in one line each
text:
34.6 Estimators and tools, in one line each







Name
One-line description




G-computation
Model the outcome, predict it under each treatment, average the difference (Chapter 6).


IPTW
Weight patients by the inverse of their treatment probability to mimic a trial (Chapter 7).


AIPW
Combine the outcome and treatment models so either one being right suffices (Chapter 8).


TMLE
A doubly robust substitution estimator that updates the outcome model and stays in the valid range (Chapter 8).


Super Learner
A cross-validated ensemble that picks the best blend of candidate algorithms (Chapter 9).


HAL
A flexible learner with a convergence guarantee targeted learning can rely on (Chapter 10).


L-TMLE
TMLE extended to multiple time points with time-varying confounding (Chapter 14).


LMTP
Longitudinal modified treatment policies: realistic, support-respecting interventions (Chapter 20).

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35 Annotated Bibliography
Key readings in modern causal inference, targeted learning, and real-world evidence generation. Each annotation summarizes why the paper matters and what it contributes.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
section: 35.1 Causal Roadmap and Target Trial Emulation
text:
35.1 Causal Roadmap and Target Trial Emulation
Petersen & van der Laan (2014) – Causal models and learning from data: integrating causal modeling and statistical estimation. Epidemiology 25(3):418-426. The foundational paper introducing the Causal Roadmap as a structured framework for causal analysis. Emphasizes the separation of causal question, identification, and estimation.
Dang et al. (2023) – A causal roadmap for generating high-quality real-world evidence. J Clin Transl Sci 7(1):e127. Extends the roadmap to RWE settings with explicit data quality assessment and reporting requirements.
Hernan & Robins (2016) – Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 183(8):758-764. Defines target trial emulation, a cornerstone idea for translating causal inference to observational study design.
Hernan & Robins (2025) – Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC. The standard graduate textbook for causal inference. Covers potential outcomes, DAGs, g-methods, and longitudinal causal inference. Freely available online.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.2 Estimand Framework
ICH E9(R1) Addendum (2020) – Estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials. Establishes the estimand framework to align trial objectives, analyses, and interpretations. Defines intercurrent event strategies.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.3 Core Estimation Methods
Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983) – The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika 70(1):41-55. The foundational propensity score paper. Establishes balancing properties and conditions for valid causal inference using propensity scores.
van der Laan & Rubin (2006) – Targeted maximum likelihood learning. Int J Biostat 2(1):Article 11. The original TMLE paper. Introduces the targeting step that makes substitution estimators doubly robust and efficient.
van der Laan, Polley & Hubbard (2007) – Super Learner. Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol 6(1). Introduces ensemble learning via cross-validation for optimal prediction. The oracle inequality guarantees asymptotic optimality relative to the best combination of candidates.
van der Laan & Rose (2011) – Targeted Learning: Causal Inference for Observational and Experimental Data. Springer. The comprehensive reference for the targeted learning framework, covering TMLE, Super Learner, and their theoretical foundations.
Zheng & van der Laan (2011) – Cross-validated targeted minimum-loss-based estimation. In Targeted Learning, Springer. Introduces CV-TMLE, which relaxes Donsker-class conditions for valid inference when using data-adaptive learners.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.4 Longitudinal Methods
Robins, Hernan & Brumback (2000) – Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 11(5):550-560. The paper that introduced marginal structural models and IPTW for longitudinal data with time-varying confounding.
Petersen et al. (2014) – Targeted maximum likelihood estimation for dynamic and static longitudinal marginal structural working models. J Causal Inference 2(2):147-185. Extends TMLE to the longitudinal setting with multiple time points, time-varying confounders, and static or dynamic regimes.
Diaz et al. (2023) – Nonparametric causal effects based on longitudinal modified treatment policies. JASA 118(542):846-856. Introduces the LMTP framework for realistic longitudinal interventions that depend on the natural treatment value. Enables feasible shift interventions that respect positivity.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.5 Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis
Sterne et al. (2016) – ROBINS-I: a tool for assessing risk of bias in non-randomised studies of interventions. BMJ 355:i4919. The standard risk-of-bias assessment tool for observational studies. Organizes bias into domains (confounding, selection, measurement, reporting).
VanderWeele & Ding (2017) – Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value. Ann Intern Med 167(4):268-274. Introduces E-values for quantifying robustness to unmeasured confounding on the risk ratio scale.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.6 Regulatory Guidance
FDA (2018) – Framework for FDA’s Real-World Evidence Program. Establishes the regulatory framework for using RWD/RWE in regulatory decisions.
FDA (2023) – Considerations for the Design and Conduct of Externally Controlled Trials. Guidance on external control arms, comparability assessment, and sensitivity analysis.

title: 34  Annotated Bibliography
text:
35.7 Suggested Reading Order

Hernan & Robins (2025) and Petersen & van der Laan (2014) for conceptual grounding
van der Laan et al. (2007) and van der Laan & Rubin (2006) for estimation
Diaz et al. (2023) and Petersen et al. (2014) for longitudinal methods

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36 Other Resources
External textbooks, courses, software, and reference sites for causal inference and targeted learning. The list favours freely available, actively maintained resources.

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.1 Foundational textbooks (free online)

Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If – The standard graduate text. Potential outcomes, DAGs, g-methods, and longitudinal causal inference, with the full PDF available at no cost.
van der Laan & Rose, Targeted Learning (2011) and Targeted Learning in Data Science (2018) – The comprehensive references for the TMLE and Super Learner framework.
Kennedy, Semiparametric doubly robust targeted double machine learning: a review (2022) – A concise modern review of the efficiency theory behind doubly robust and targeted estimators, for readers who want the theory behind the influence-function machinery.

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.2 Online courses and interactive tutorials

Beyond the ATE – Interactive workshop on modified treatment policies and the lmtp package (Nick Williams and Iván Díaz).
TLverse Handbook (Targeted Learning in R) – Book-length guide to the targeted-learning software ecosystem (sl3, tmle3, origami, hal9001).
Introduction to Modern Causal Inference – Accessible, code-first introduction to causal inference concepts (Alejandro Schuler).
Visual Guides to Causal Inference – Illustrated guides to TMLE, Super Learner, and modified treatment policies (Katherine Hoffman).
Causal Diagrams: Draw Your Assumptions Before Your Conclusions – Free Harvard/edX course on DAGs (Miguel Hernán).
Introduction to Causal Inference – Free lecture course with downloadable notes (Brady Neal).
A Crash Course in Causality – Free Coursera course on confounding, IPW, and g-methods for an epidemiology audience (Jason Roy).

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.3 Applied complements

Causal Inference: The Mixtape – Applied, econometrics-flavoured treatment of causal designs (Scott Cunningham).
Causal Inference for the Brave and True – Python-based applied causal inference handbook (Matheus Facure).

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.4 Software
Maintenance and channel status below are current as of mid-2026; because that status is the most perishable part of any software list, confirm a package’s version and channel before relying on it. A fuller treatment of the targeted-learning package landscape, with versions, download counts, and recommendations by estimand, is given in the TMLE software scoping review (Mertens and colleagues).
Core estimators (R, on CRAN).

tmle – point-treatment ATE, risk ratio, odds ratio, and marginal structural model parameters; the reference implementation.
drtmle – point-treatment counterfactual means with doubly robust inference (intervals stay valid when one nuisance converges slowly).
ltmle – longitudinal TMLE for time-varying treatment and confounding; reports the g-computation and IPW estimates alongside the targeted one.
lmtp – longitudinal modified treatment policies (static, dynamic, and feasible shifts), point and longitudinal, including survival with competing risks. Released under AGPL-3, which can matter for closed-source or commercial reuse.
txshift – population mean under an additive shift of a continuous exposure, with two-phase sampling.
SuperLearner – cross-validated ensemble for nuisance estimation.

Specialized settings.

Survival and competing risks: survtmle (discrete-time cumulative incidence) and concrete (continuous-time absolute risk). Both are archived from CRAN and now install from GitHub; lmtp is the maintained CRAN alternative for survival with competing risks.
Mediation: crumble and medoutcon – interventional direct and indirect effects (GitHub).
Near-positivity violations: ctmle – collaborative TMLE (CRAN; not updated since 2019, so confirm it builds).
Optimal individualized rules: tmle3mopttx – the only dedicated targeted-learning implementation (GitHub / r-universe). For exploratory CATE, grf and policytree.
Combining a trial with real-world data: EScvtmle (experiment-selector CV-TMLE) and atmle (adaptive TMLE; GitHub).
High-dimensional biomarker importance: biotmle (Bioconductor).

Infrastructure (R).

hal9001 – highly adaptive lasso (Chapter 10); origami – cross-validation; haldensify – HAL conditional density estimation for shift-intervention nuisances. The tlverse ecosystem (sl3, tmle3) ties these together.

Python.

causalml and zEpid – point-treatment TMLE for the ATE; pytmle – survival and competing risks. No Python package yet spans longitudinal, modified-treatment-policy, mediation, or high-dimensional estimands, so use the R tools for those.

Other environments.

Stata: the contributed eltmle command (point-treatment ATE).

Diagnostics and sensitivity (used in this handbook).

EValue, episensr, ipw.

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.5 Research groups

UC Berkeley Center for Targeted Machine Learning and Causal Inference (CTML) – Center developing the methods and software in this handbook.
CAUSALab, Harvard – Target-trial emulation and g-methods.

title: 35  Other Resources
text:
36.6 Workshops and community

TMLE Workshop (Ehsan Karim) – Applied TMLE workshop materials with R code.
American Causal Inference Conference (ACIC) – Annual meeting of the Society for Causal Inference.
